Afghanistan.d:
Afghanistan's governments have long been run in part by people that foreign powers paid, trained or protected, and Pakistan's military intelligence service, the ISI, has reached furthest. Since the Taliban took Kabul in 2021, the interior ministry and Kabul's security have been run by the Haqqani network, a militant group inside the Taliban that the top US military officer once called an arm of the ISI. Pakistan denies interfering.

Before 2021 the reach came through cash and agents. For more than a decade the CIA delivered bags of money to President Hamid Karzai's office, tens of millions of dollars that went on to relatives, politicians and warlords, and Iran's government paid his chief of staff in the same way; Karzai confirmed both. In 2012 the Afghan intelligence service told parliament it had arrested 15 government employees, including senior officials and a general, for spying for the ISI or Iran. The drug trade reached in too: the official in charge of fighting it was accused of using his post to give smugglers safe passage.

For people living there, the police in the capital answer to a faction accused of serving a neighbouring spy service, and for twenty years the men around the president were kept loyal with foreign money rather than by voters. The Global Organized Crime Index scores Afghanistan 9 out of 10 for officials working for criminal or outside interests and 1.5 for courts, police and watchdogs, so residents have almost nowhere to take a complaint.

Angola.d:
Angola's state runs mainly on oil, and the state oil company, Sonangol, which awards offshore contracts, is where foreign firms have reached in most often. Oil traders, builders of oil platforms, construction groups and a management consultancy have all paid Angolan officials through local agents and bank accounts abroad to win state business, and the reach goes beyond oil to public works, the Ministry of the Economy and the central bank. The clearest view comes from the Dutch platform builder SBM Offshore, which admitted that from 1997 to 2012 the 'commissions' it paid its Angolan agents were passed on to at least nine Sonangol officials. Most of what is known comes from admissions and court cases in Switzerland and the United States; the Angolan officials who took the money are mostly unnamed.

The same pattern ran through the rebuilding of the country after its civil war. China International Fund, a Hong Kong company, ran Chinese-financed reconstruction in partnership with generals close to the former president José Eduardo dos Santos, and in 2022 Angolan prosecutors indicted two of those generals and the company, alleging that money meant for public housing went to private ends and that about $1.5 billion in Chinese payments for Angolan oil never reached Angola. The generals went on trial in 2024.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Angola 8 out of 10 for officials working for criminal or outside interests and about 4 out of 10 for the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs. For Angolans, this means the oil revenue and foreign loans that should pay for housing, schools, hospitals and wages have repeatedly been split with foreign companies and well-placed officers, and most of the officials paid have never been named at home.

Australia.d:
In Australia outsiders reach in through three main routes: crime groups buying police and border officers, foreign governments cultivating politicians, and industries placing their people where policy is shaped.

The police route is the oldest. Public inquiries in Queensland in the late 1980s and New South Wales in the mid-1990s found that brothel, illegal casino and drug operators paid officers as a matter of routine. The buying has since moved to the border: drug importers in Sydney and Melbourne recruit 'trusted insiders' in Border Force, the state police and freight firms to keep their parcels and containers from being inspected, and in 2024 federal and state police formed a strike team just to find them.

Foreign governments work through people. A donor tied to China's United Front, the Chinese Communist Party office that organises influence abroad through community groups, paid a senator's bills, and the senator then backed China's line against his own party's policy. India's foreign intelligence service has cultivated politicians, ASIO, the domestic security agency, says another country's spies recruited a former politician, and an army private is charged with obtaining defence information for Russia.

Firms reach the policy end. A PwC partner hired by the Treasury to advise on laws against multinational tax avoidance passed its plans to colleagues advising the companies targeted, and in 2020 gas and mining executives ran the commission planning the Covid recovery. For people here, the officer checking cargo may be paid by the trade they are meant to stop, and tax and energy policy can be shaped by those it affects.

Bahrain.d:
Bahrain is a small Gulf kingdom whose largest industry outside oil is aluminium, and its documented case of outsiders reaching in runs through the state-controlled smelter, Aluminium Bahrain, known as Alba. To keep long-term contracts to supply Alba with alumina, the raw material for aluminium, the US company Alcoa placed a London-based middleman with close ties to senior members of the royal family between itself and the smelter. Sales went through his offshore companies, which marked up prices by about $188 million between 2005 and 2009, and he used that margin to pay tens of millions of dollars in kickbacks to the Bahraini officials who controlled the tenders. Alcoa's subsidiary pleaded guilty to bribery in the United States in 2014.

Bahrain's politics are also shaped by the rivalry between Sunni-led Gulf states and Shia Iran. The Muslim Brotherhood, a Sunni Islamist movement active across the Arab world, has a documented presence; groups allied with Iran's Revolutionary Guards are thought to be present but are not documented inside the state. The Global Organized Crime Index scores Bahrain 4.5 out of 10 for officials working for criminal or outside interests and about 5.3 out of 10 for the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs, both in the middle of the range.

For Bahrainis, this means a state company that belongs to the public paid inflated prices for its raw material for years, and the difference went to the officials running its tenders and the middleman connected to the royal family. The case was brought by a foreign court, and the officials who took the money have not been named at home.

Belgium.d:
Belgium is where outsiders reach into Europe and the Western alliance as a whole. Brussels hosts the main EU institutions and NATO's headquarters, and Antwerp is the port through which more cocaine reaches Europe than any other, so foreign governments, companies and drug networks all have reasons to get people inside.

Spy services have worked to place or recruit people on NATO's own staff for decades. Soviet and East German intelligence had long-term agents inside it during the Cold War, and in 2026 an intern in the IT department of NATO's military headquarters at Mons was arrested on suspicion of spying, reportedly for China. Hungarian spies have tried to recruit Hungarians working at the European Commission, Hungary's foreign minister has been reported phoning Russia's foreign minister from breaks in closed EU meetings, which he says passed no secrets, and Morocco placed its own people in charge of Brussels' Great Mosque and inside Belgium's official Muslim body.

Gulf money reaches the people who negotiate and vote. Belgian prosecutors say Qatar and Morocco paid cash to members of the European Parliament in a case known as Qatargate; the accused deny it. Prosecutors also suspect lobbyists for a Chinese telecoms company of paying MEPs to oppose limits on foreign 5G equipment.

In Antwerp, cocaine networks pay port workers, terminal staff, customs officers and police to pull containers out and pass on access codes, and an investigating judge wrote in 2025 that inquiries had also led to arrests of municipal clerks and justice staff in prisons and the courthouse. For people in Belgium and across the EU, this means rules on trade, technology and human rights may have been shaped by foreign payments, and the clerks, guards and officers handling their cases may work for the networks they are meant to stop.

Bolivia.d:
Bolivia is one of the world's main producers of coca, the plant cocaine is made from, and for more than forty years traffickers have bought the part of the state meant to stop them: the interior ministry, the anti-drug police and the offices that issue documents. The pattern took shape in the 1980 'Cocaine Coup', when the leading trafficker helped pay for a military takeover and his cousin became interior minister, in charge of the police. Twice in recent years a former head of the anti-narcotics police, the FELCN, has been convicted in the United States of working for traffickers, protecting cocaine loads and steering investigations away from allied gangs.

Foreign traffickers now use the same openings. The Uruguayan cocaine boss Sebastián Marset lived openly in Santa Cruz from 2022, bought a football club, travelled on a false Bolivian identity card that an employee of the national identification service issued him, and slipped away from a police raid in 2023, apparently warned; he was caught only in 2026. Earlier, foreign intelligence and secret officers' groups reached the top: an interior minister of the 1960s said the CIA had recruited him, and in 1943 a secret faction of army officers put one of its members in the presidency.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Bolivia 6.5 out of 10 for officials working for criminal interests and about 4.6 for its courts, police and watchdogs. For people living there, the police unit they would turn to about a trafficking gang has repeatedly been run by someone on a gang's payroll, and investigations have been pointed away from favoured traffickers and towards their rivals. Both convictions of anti-drug chiefs came from US courts, not Bolivian ones.

Brunei.d:
Nothing is documented yet for Brunei, so this is an estimate based on conditions. No case found so far shows a foreign intelligence service, company, crime group, church or lodge paying or placing people inside its government.

Brunei is a small, oil-rich sultanate on Borneo where the sultan holds executive power and there is no elected parliament, so there are few public channels through which outside influence would come to light. The Global Organized Crime Index scores Brunei 3 out of 10 for officials working for criminal or outside interests, low by world standards, and about 4.6 out of 10 for resilience, meaning the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs.

For people living there, this means there is no documented case of an official acting for an outside interest, and the low score suggests the risk is small. With few public channels and middling oversight, though, such a case would be hard to bring to light, and a documented case would change this estimate.

Cabo Verde.d:
Little is documented for Cabo Verde, so this is an estimate. No case found so far shows a foreign state, company, criminal group or lodge paying or placing people inside its government. The Global Organized Crime Index rates the country low for officials working for criminal interests and comparatively strong in its courts, police and watchdogs, which suggests fewer officials act for outside interests here than in most of West Africa. The islands sit on Atlantic shipping lanes between South America, West Africa and Europe, so the ports are the place most exposed to outside money.

The lack of cases may also reflect how little investigative reporting covers the islands. If outside money does reach officials, it would most likely show up in the ports, in shipping and in public contracts, and residents would pay for it through lost public revenue rather than through anything they could see directly. For now there is no named official, company or group for Cabo Verdeans to hold to account.

Central African Republic.d:
In the Central African Republic a foreign armed group works from inside the state. Wagner, the Russian private military company tied to Yevgeny Prigozhin, arrived in 2018 and placed its own people in the presidency: one of its men, Valery Zakharov, served as President Touadéra's national security adviser and was sanctioned by the United States for his Wagner ties. A US-sponsored research centre, the Africa Center for Strategic Studies, assesses that the old Wagner organisation has in effect taken over the state.

The arrangement has spread into the drug trade. Reporting from Bangui in 2026 describes Wagner's remnants supplying tramadol, an opioid painkiller, to members of the presidential guard and to a youth militia, with senior security officials alleged to control the market and payments flowing to Wagner and allied armed groups along the smuggling route. No one has been charged.

For people in the country, the president's security advice has come from a Wagner man answerable to Moscow rather than to Central African voters or courts, and some of the armed men around them are supplied with opioids by the same network. The Global Organized Crime Index rates the country among the very worst in the world for officials working for criminal interests, with almost no capacity in its courts, police or watchdogs to resist.

Colombia.d:
In Colombia the drug trade and the armed groups built on it have reached into every level of the state for more than forty years. The cocaine cartels and the AUC, right-wing paramilitaries who were also major traffickers, got their own people elected, paid into presidential campaigns and bought the officials meant to hunt them; in the 'parapolítica' scandal about 30 per cent of Congress was investigated, charged or convicted over collusion with the paramilitaries. Traffickers have paid police, legislators and judges for protection from extradition and the courts, and two former Supreme Court presidents and the national anti-corruption prosecutor were convicted of taking money to bury cases.

The groups that took over the trade after the peace deals buy their protection closer to the ground. The Gulf Clan, the country's largest trafficking group, funds mayoral candidates along its routes, has paid police units monthly to ignore its drug sales and, prosecutors say, used a community leader as a go-between to pay soldiers for troop movements and planned operations against it. Smuggling networks do the same with the customs police, and files seized from a FARC dissident faction describe talks with an army general and an intelligence official about a front company to buy weapons, which both deny.

Companies reach in through public contracts. In 2023 an investment company in Grupo Aval, one of Colombia's main banking groups, agreed to pay more than $80 million over more than $23 million in bribes that it and Brazil's Odebrecht paid officials and lawmakers for a toll-road contract.

For Colombians, this has meant voting for mayors whose campaigns traffickers helped fund, reporting crimes to officers who may be on a group's payroll, and soldiers going into operations the other side already knew about. Most of this became known through Colombia's own courts.

Costa Rica.d:
Costa Rica lies on the route that carries Colombian cocaine north to the United States and across to Europe, and traffickers keep that route open by recruiting people inside the police and the security ministry to tell them what investigators know. The clearest case reaches near the top: the US Treasury found that a former vice-minister of public security, who later sat as a judge, helped move cocaine through the country and used his government contacts to learn about open drug investigations. He was arrested on a US extradition request in 2025 and has not been convicted.

The same method runs through the ranks of the national police. On the Caribbean side, trafficking groups have recruited local officers as lookouts to warn them of raids and checkpoints; in Guanacaste on the Pacific side, local officers have passed information to groups flying drugs out from clandestine airstrips. In 2026 the government said 116 officers of the public security ministry were under investigation after an internal intelligence report found some escorting criminals and coordinating secret drug flights.

Companies seeking public money have reached in too. Prosecutors say the two construction firms that received nearly two-thirds of the national roads agency's funds paid its staff in cash, liquor and vehicles to favour them, and 14 officials were among 30 people detained in 2021.

For people living along the cocaine routes, the officers they would call for help may be the ones telling traffickers when the police are coming, and the roads their taxes pay for may have gone to the firms that paid the agency's staff. The Global Organized Crime Index rates Costa Rica's officials as relatively unlikely to work for criminal interests, with institutions of middling strength.

Cyprus.d:
The deepest outside reach into the Cypriot state came from Greece, and its result is still the shape of the island. In the early 1970s Greece's military government had about 650 of its own officers serving in Cyprus's army, the National Guard, and it funded and controlled an armed group that wanted Cyprus joined to Greece. In July 1974, on the junta's orders, the National Guard attacked the presidential palace and overthrew President Makarios; Turkey invaded five days later and came to hold 37 per cent of the island, which remains divided.

The Global Organized Crime Index rates Cyprus low to middling for officials working for criminal interests, but its courts, police and watchdogs score weak for an EU member. For Cypriots, this means a foreign government once used officers inside their own army to remove their elected president, and they still live with the partition that followed. No later case on the map shows an outside party inside the Cypriot state, but the bodies that would find one are weaker than in most of the EU.

Dominica.d:
The one documented case of outside money reaching Dominica's government involves a campaign donation. Al Jazeera reported that an Iranian businessman gave hundreds of thousands of dollars to Prime Minister Roosevelt Skerrit's election campaign and received an ambassador's post and a diplomatic passport in return; the businessman was later jailed in Iran for stealing oil revenue. Skerrit denies any trade, and no court has ruled on the claim.

If the report is right, a post that speaks for Dominica abroad went to a campaign donor, and a diplomatic passport, which carries legal protections overseas, went to a man later jailed for theft. Dominicans have no public record of what campaign donors receive.

The Global Organized Crime Index rates Dominica low for officials working for criminal interests, with institutions of middling strength.

El Salvador.d:
In El Salvador the documented case of criminal groups reaching the state comes through local office and the drug trade. The country's two largest gangs, MS-13 and Barrio 18, grew out of Salvadoran communities in Los Angeles and now run neighbourhoods across the country, but the case on the map concerns trafficking along the northern border.

The news site El Faro reported in 2011 that a network moving drugs along that border, known as the Texis Cartel, was led by a sitting mayor, with police, soldiers, judges and prosecutors paid to let shipments through. A court acquitted all nine defendants in 2021, so the account remains a press finding rather than a proven one.

If the reporting is right, a town hall was used to move drugs, and the officers and courts that should have stopped the shipments were paid to let them pass. Salvadorans have had no court finding at home to settle it. The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal interests at 7.5 out of 10 and the strength of courts and watchdogs at 3.25.

Eswatini.d:
This is an estimate: no case on the map shows a foreign state, company, criminal group or religious body placing or paying people inside Eswatini's government. Eswatini is a small kingdom between South Africa and Mozambique where the king holds executive power and political parties cannot compete for government, so there are few independent sources inside the country that report on officials.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal or outside interests at 6.5 out of 10, in its high band, and the courts, police and watchdogs that would resist them at about 3.2. A country with that profile, on the trade routes between South Africa and Mozambique, is one where traffickers and businesses seeking contracts would find officials open to payment and little chance of a case reaching court.

If that is happening, people in Eswatini would pay for it through public contracts that cost more than they should and policing that does not reach those who pay. With no named case, there is no official, company or group they can point to or hold to account.

France.d:
In France outside interests reach government mostly through the people who run it and the money behind their campaigns. Some officials act for a firm from inside the offices that set policy: leaked Uber documents show Emmanuel Macron, as economy minister in 2015, working behind the scenes for Uber, and a police ban on its service was lifted after his office was contacted. A former investment banker in the president's office followed a bank merger he had advised on and then took charge of the merged bank; he was prosecuted and acquitted.

Campaign money is the second channel, much of it from abroad; in 2025 Nicolas Sarkozy was sentenced to prison for conspiring with Gaddafi's intelligence chief to seek Libyan money for his 2007 campaign; he is appealing.

Foreign spy services and crime groups work on insiders lower down, and sometimes inside France's own intelligence service. Chinese intelligence obtained secrets from two officers of the DGSE, the foreign intelligence agency, and both were jailed in 2020. Prosecutors say Algeria's consulate near Paris obtained information on asylum seekers and government opponents from a finance ministry employee. Cocaine networks pay or threaten the staff who control the main entry points: dockers at Le Havre, who move containers and lend security badges, and, the gendarmerie says, employees and managers of a company working at Roissy-Charles-de-Gaulle airport.

For people in France, rules on taxi services or banking may have been shaped by a firm before ministers present them, an Algerian who fled to France cannot be sure their file stays inside the French state, and some of the people handling cargo at the port and airport work for the networks shipping drugs through them. The Global Organized Crime Index rates officials acting for criminal interests low and the courts strong.

Germany.d:
Germany has been a main target for foreign intelligence services since the Cold War, and they work by placing or recruiting people inside its institutions. East Germany's Stasi had a personal aide to Chancellor Willy Brandt, whose exposure in 1974 brought Brandt down, and agents in parliament and in the foreign intelligence service, the BND. Since Russia's full invasion of Ukraine more cases involve the armed forces and their supply routes. Russia's services are accused of running a BND officer and reported to have tasked an AfD MP's aide in the Bundestag, and a captain in the army's procurement office was jailed for taking internal files to Russia's consulate. China's had an aide in an MEP's office who drew on a logistics worker at Leipzig airport, a cargo hub for military shipments, for details of arms and troop flights. Foreign money reaches parliament too: several conservative MPs have resigned or been investigated over payments from Azerbaijan.

Companies reach in through people and paperwork. The energy minister appointed in 2025 came straight from running E.ON's largest subsidiary and has since planned more gas power and less support for rooftop solar. Germany's risk agency copied large parts of the glyphosate makers' own application into the safety review the EU used to renew the weedkiller, and at Hamburg and Bremerhaven cocaine importers recruit customs officers and terminal staff to clear containers.

For people in Germany, critics of Moscow and Beijing live alongside people those governments have recruited in parliament and the army, and decisions on energy and farm chemicals have rested partly on people and text from the firms affected. The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal interests at 2 out of 10 and courts and watchdogs above 7, so most of these cases are investigated and many reach court.

Guatemala.d:
Guatemala's state has been reached from outside for seventy years, first by a foreign intelligence service and now by drug traffickers and companies seeking public contracts. In 1954 the CIA put an exiled officer on its payroll and sent him in to overthrow the elected president, whose land reform had taken land from the US-based United Fruit Company, and it kept paid sources in the army afterwards.

Today the country lies on the land route that carries South American cocaine north, and the groups that use it buy officials at every level the drugs pass through. Since 2005 the people charged or convicted for working with traffickers have included the head of the anti-narcotics police, a town mayor who used his office's letterhead to get cocaine past inspection, a member of Congress, and a vice-president and interior minister. Gangs reach the prisons: in October 2025, 23 guards were arrested for helping 20 Barrio 18 gang leaders walk out of a high-security jail.

Foreign builders have paid their way in at the top as well. Prosecutors and the former UN-backed anti-impunity commission say bribes from the Brazilian construction company Odebrecht to win a highway expansion were managed by the minister in charge of public works, who kept about $9 million himself and has been ordered to stand trial.

For Guatemalans this means the police officer, mayor or legislator they would turn to may be working for traffickers, at times the agency meant to stop cocaine has helped move it, and the roads their taxes pay for have been awarded by a minister accused of taking the builder's money. The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal interests at 8 out of 10 and courts and watchdogs at 4.

Haiti.d:
In Haiti armed gangs control much of the capital, Port-au-Prince, and large areas of the Artibonite valley, and the line between the gangs and the state has worn thin from both sides. Politicians have funded and armed gangs to control territory and voters. Canada and the United States have sanctioned a former president, sitting and former senators and other political figures for financing gangs, and a UN panel of experts says former legislators have armed groups and used them to drive violence before elections. Those named deny it.

The gangs in turn reach into the state. The UN panel reported in October 2026 that some police officers supply gangs with weapons and information, and that at least one member of the new municipal commission in Cité Soleil, one of the capital's poorest districts, is an active gang member. Cocaine traffickers have bought protection at the top of the police for three decades, from the police chief of the 1990s military regime, indicted in the US over Colombian bribes, to a former commander who admitted taking millions to protect shipments, and the US Treasury says Michel Martelly worked with traffickers as president, which he denies.

Outside control of the state is old here: from 1915 a New York bank, the forerunner of Citigroup, owned Haiti's national bank and, under US occupation, ran its finances for decades. For people in Haiti today, the gangs that kill, kidnap and drive them from their homes are paid for by some of the politicians asking for their votes and supplied by some of the police meant to protect them. With courts and watchdogs scoring 2.2 out of 10 on the Global Organized Crime Index and officials acting for criminal interests at 8.5, none of the sanctioned politicians has faced a Haitian court.

India.d:
India's governing party is closely tied to one organisation. The Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) is a Hindu nationalist volunteer body; it trains full-time organisers and lends them to the governing Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), and it places one of its own organisers in the party's top organisational post, where he makes sure the party carries out the RSS chief's instructions. By the press's count about seven in ten BJP ministers have RSS roots, and RSS-family groups have had their own people put in charge of public bodies, from the national history research council to the prosecution of riot cases in which their members were accused.

Money and crime reach the state from other sides. Crime groups buy insiders where it pays: an illegal betting app run from Dubai is accused of paying Chhattisgarh's police and politicians, and a gang selling leaked papers got into the 2024 national medical entrance exam through the officials running one test centre. Firms have paid for contracts: US prosecutors allege the Adani Group paid Indian officials more than $250 million to win solar power contracts.

Pakistan's military intelligence service, the ISI, keeps recruiting at every level of India's defence establishment: naval sailors, a diplomat, a defence laboratory director, an engineer at the centre that builds the BrahMos cruise missile, and recently an armed-police officer in Kashmir, a clerk at navy headquarters and the manager of a guest house where weapons scientists stay during missile tests.

For people in India this means most of the ministers who draft their laws come from an organisation that publishes no membership list, large public contracts have been won, prosecutors say, by paying the officials who award them, and a student's place at medical college can depend on whether a gang has bought the officials guarding the exam papers.

Ireland.d:
For much of the twentieth century, the outsiders inside Irish government were organised bodies of men from Ireland itself, working in private: a secret republican brotherhood and then Catholic organisations. The Irish Republican Brotherhood, an oath-bound society, re-formed as a faction holding posts inside the new national army, and the fight over its grip on those posts led to a mutiny in 1924.

After independence the Catholic Church reached further. The Knights of Saint Columbanus, a secretive Catholic men's order, had a member running the justice ministry in the 1948 government, who reportedly gave the order's council private undertakings on government conduct. In 1951 the cabinet dropped the Mother and Child Scheme, a plan for free health care for mothers and children, after the Catholic bishops privately objected; the health minister resigned.

In recent decades the documented reach has come from money and, more recently, from foreign intelligence. An official tribunal found in 2011 that the businessman Denis O'Brien made payments to the minister who 'delivered' him the country's second mobile phone licence, findings O'Brien rejects. In 2024 a newspaper reported that Russian intelligence had recruited a serving member of the Oireachtas, Ireland's parliament, during the Brexit talks; the person was not named, ministers said they had not been told, and nothing has been proven.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Ireland 4 out of 10 for officials working for criminal or outside interests and above 7 for its courts and watchdogs. For people in Ireland, that history meant decisions on their families' health care were made in private letters between bishops and ministers, and it means a valuable public licence can be decided by a minister acting for a businessman, while voters have no way of knowing whether the reported Russian recruit still sits in parliament.

Japan.d:
In Japan, outside interests reach the governing Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) by supplying what a party in power needs: money, organised votes and campaign workers. The pattern goes back to the party's early years, when the CIA secretly funded it and recruited informers inside it in the 1950s and 1960s. Since then companies have repeatedly paid the men at the top, in the clearest case the US aircraft maker Lockheed, which paid about ¥500 million to Prime Minister Kakuei Tanaka's office to sell jets to a Japanese airline.

Religious movements and lobbies supply votes and volunteers: Komeito, the party of the Buddhist lay movement Soka Gakkai, governed alongside the LDP for most of 1999 to 2025. Nippon Kaigi, a lobby that wants to rewrite the post-war constitution, and the political arm of the Shinto shrines each run a league of MPs that has counted most cabinet ministers under recent prime ministers.

Foreign spy services and crime groups work lower down, by recruiting individual staff inside companies and the police. Russian intelligence officers posted to their country's trade mission have paid employees of a mobile network and of a machine-tool maker whose products can have military uses for internal files and trade secrets. In 2025 a detective in Tokyo's organised-crime division was arrested for sending a large 'scout' gang, which recruits women for sex parlours, the locations of the cameras police had set up to watch it.

For people in Japan, this means those they elect may owe their campaigns to a company with a contract at stake, ministers belong to lobbies whose membership the government does not disclose, an inquiry into a gang can be leaked to it from inside the police, and, as an inquiry found after Fukushima, a regulator can end up serving the power companies it polices.

Kiribati.d:
No case on this map documents a foreign state, criminal group or company paying or placing officials inside Kiribati's government, so this account rests on general conditions.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Kiribati low, 1.5 out of 10, for officials working for criminal interests, but below 5 for the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs. A weak oversight score means there are few institutions in a position to notice outside influence if it came.

For people in Kiribati this means the risk that officials are serving criminal interests appears low, but the means of checking are thin. If outside influence did reach their government, it would most likely show in fishing licences, aid-funded contracts or policing, and with limited courts and press it could go unexamined.

Kuwait.d:
Outside interests reach into Kuwait's government by three routes on the record: an Islamist movement working openly in politics, foreign businesses paying the officials who control visas and arms purchases, and Iran recruiting inside the army.

The Muslim Brotherhood, a Sunni Islamist movement founded in Egypt that aims to bring its members into power, has a Kuwaiti branch that broke with the international organisation after Iraq invaded in 1990. Its party, the Islamic Constitutional Movement, regularly won seats in parliament through the 1990s and 2000s and at times sent members into the cabinet.

Foreign suppliers have paid officials directly. A Bangladeshi member of parliament whose companies supplied cleaners for government contracts was convicted in 2021, alongside a senior Interior Ministry general, of paying ministry officials to issue visas for more than 20,000 workers, some on fake papers. A parliamentary inquiry in 2024 found that a European helicopter maker paid commissions on a defence contract and named eight senior officials, though parliament was dissolved before any prosecution. In 2011 a Kuwaiti court convicted soldiers serving in the army of passing military information to Iran's Revolutionary Guards.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Kuwait 6 out of 10 for officials working for criminal interests and just over 5 for its courts and watchdogs. For Kuwaitis this means the officials who decide who may live and work in the country, and those who spend the defence budget, have been paid by foreign suppliers, while migrant workers brought in on bought visas carry the cost. The inquiry into the helicopter deal put the public money wasted at €349 million.

Lebanon.d:
In Lebanon, foreign states have reached into the government for much of the past seventy years, mostly by choosing who sits in it. In the 1957 election CIA officers carried cash to the president's chosen candidates, so the parliament that resulted was largely made up of members the agency had paid for.

From 1982 Syria's military intelligence chief in Lebanon picked electoral candidates, drew electoral districts and shaped security and judicial appointments, and the head of Lebanon's General Security agency reported to him. This lasted until Syrian troops left in 2005.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Lebanon 9.5 out of 10 for officials working for criminal or outside interests and about 3 for its courts and watchdogs, close to the worst in the world. For people in Lebanon this means that for long stretches the members they elected, and the officials running their security services and courts, were chosen or paid for by a foreign government.

Liechtenstein.d:
Liechtenstein is a small principality between Switzerland and Austria whose banks and trust companies hold money for foreign clients. No documented case yet meets the map's test there: none shows a foreign government, crime group or company getting its people or money inside Liechtenstein's government or courts and steering what they decided.

The Global Organized Crime Index places Liechtenstein among the countries where officials are least likely to work for criminal or outside interests, and rates its courts, police and watchdogs as strong.

For people who live in Liechtenstein, this means the officials they deal with are rated as rarely acting for someone else. If the risk grows, it is most likely to sit in the banks and trustees that manage foreign money and in the officials who supervise them.

Malawi.d:
In Malawi, the documented outside reach is through the procurement of the country's security forces, where a single foreign supplier is alleged to have bought his way into contracts with the police and the army. Malawi's anti-corruption bureau reported in 2022 that companies linked to Zuneth Sattar, a UK-based businessman, won contracts worth more than 150 million dollars from both forces over four years, and that he paid officials to secure them. The bureau's report named dozens of people, and arrests reached a former police chief, a cabinet minister and the vice president, who denied wrongdoing and died in a plane crash in 2024. These are findings and arrests, not convictions.

The mechanism is common where security spending is large and kept away from public scrutiny: the buyer is the state, the details are confidential on security grounds, and one well-connected supplier can win repeated contracts if the officials signing them are paid. The Global Organized Crime Index rates Malawi's institutions as weak and finds a moderate level of officials serving outside interests.

For Malawians this means that tax money meant to equip the police and army went, through contracts the bureau says were bought, to the companies of one outside supplier, with the alleged payments reaching as far as the vice president's office. The cases have not been decided, so people still do not know who in their government took part or what the public received for the money.

Malta.d:
In Malta, outside interests have reached the state in two ways: through private companies that win large state contracts with help from the people closest to the prime minister, and through the licences Malta grants to firms that then operate across the European Union.

The clearest example of the first is the gas power station built under a state contract. One of the builder's directors secretly owned a company in Dubai that leaked papers listed as expected to pay into secret Panama companies set up for the energy minister and the prime minister's chief of staff; the journalist Daphne Caruana Galizia was investigating that company when a car bomb killed her in 2017, and the director now faces trial over her murder while all three men face corruption charges. A public inquiry found that the Maltese state had created an 'atmosphere of impunity'.

The second channel runs through Malta's online gambling industry. Because a Maltese licence lets a betting firm operate across the EU, Italian mafia groups, including the 'Ndrangheta from Calabria and Cosa Nostra from Sicily, have secretly owned or run Malta-licensed betting companies to collect bets and launder money, according to Italian investigations over the past decade. Malta's regulator suspended licences once the investigations surfaced.

For people in Malta this means they pay for electricity from a plant whose contract prosecutors say was tied to payments meant for the two men around the prime minister, and the reporter who tried to expose it was killed. It also means their country's licences have served as cover for mafias, and the Global Organized Crime Index finds officials there often serving criminal or outside interests.

Mexico.d:
In Mexico, drug cartels have put officials on their payroll at every level of government for more than forty years. Where a cartel controls a route or a town, it pays the local police, the prosecutors who decide which cases go forward and in several states the governor. Those hired to fight the cartels have been bought most often: the national anti-drug chief, generals, agents in the federal organised-crime unit, prison directors and a federal security minister.

The town hall is where the buying is most common today. Whole municipal police forces have been disbanded because they worked for cartels, and a federal operation begun in 2024 had detained more than 85 officials, including at least 19 mayors, across nine states by mid-2026. Some town halls are accused of working for a cartel's business: in 2026 the mayor of Tequila, in Jalisco, was arrested with his security director, accused of running an extortion ring tied to the Jalisco New Generation Cartel that squeezed drinks makers with inflated taxes and withheld permits.

The reach extends to the ports and the money system. Fuel importers are accused of paying navy officers and customs staff to let tankers of diesel declared as additives dock uninspected and untaxed. The US Treasury said in 2025 that staff at two Mexican banks had helped cartels launder money, which Mexico's finance ministry and the banks dispute. Foreign companies have also paid officials at Pemex, the state oil company, and at other state bodies.

For Mexicans this means the police officer, mayor or governor they depend on may be working for the people they should be stopping, a firm may be taxed by its town hall on a cartel's behalf, and fuel that should be taxed to pay for public services is waved through at the docks.

Mongolia.d:
Nothing is documented of a foreign state, company, crime group or religious body paying or placing people inside Mongolia's government, so this is an estimate based on conditions.

Mongolia sits between Russia and China, its two large neighbours and main trading routes. The Global Organized Crime Index finds a moderate level of officials serving criminal or outside interests and rates its courts, police and watchdogs in the middle range. A country with that profile is one where outside money could reach some officials, most likely through licences and public contracts, but where institutions have some capacity to notice and respond.

For people in Mongolia this means there is no named official, company or group acting for an outside interest that they can point to or hold to account. The estimate rests on the index's assessment rather than on any inquiry or court ruling, and a documented case would change it.

Myanmar.d:
In Myanmar the army has drawn armed crime groups into the state itself, trading protection and business for their loyalty. Along the borders with China and Thailand, militias the army has formally placed under its command, and armed groups allied with it, control the parts of Shan and Karen states that produce much of Asia's methamphetamine and host compounds where trafficked workers are forced to defraud strangers online. Their leaders hold military rank and state honours while partnering with Chinese-run crime groups and letting them build on the land their forces hold; the commander of the Karen Border Guard Force helped build the scam city of Shwe Kokko and received a top state honour, and the UK and US have since sanctioned him.

A Buddhist nationalist monks' group, Ma Ba Tha, reached into lawmaking. The religious affairs ministry drafted four 'race and religion' laws from texts its members proposed, and parliament passed them in 2015. They restrict religious conversion and marriage between Buddhist women and non-Buddhist men.

The Global Organized Crime Index finds Myanmar's officials serving criminal interests to one of the highest degrees in the world, with almost no court or police capacity to check them. For people in Shan and Karen states this means living beside drug labs and guarded compounds run by forces the army counts as its own. Muslim residents and Buddhist women live under marriage and conversion rules drawn from a monks' movement's drafts.

Netherlands.d:
In the Netherlands, outsiders reach in at three points: cocaine gangs work through the people who move goods and handle information, foreign states have sought people inside the International Criminal Court in The Hague and the country's nuclear technology, and a foreign company once paid an insider to sway a government purchase.

At Rotterdam, Europe's largest port, they have paid terminal workers and IT contractors for the PIN codes that release containers, private security guards to keep searches away, and a customs officer whose job was choosing which containers get scanned. At Schiphol airport they recruit staff whose passes let them move freight past controls. They also buy information from inside the state: police officers and trainees have searched police systems for gangs at a set price per name, and court staff with access to personal records have sold them to suspects. Courts have convicted such insiders many times, and gangs that rely on them have killed people connected to trials against them.

The Hague hosts the International Criminal Court, which tries war crimes, and Russia has tried to get inside it. In 2022 a Russian military intelligence officer with a false Brazilian identity flew in to take up a post there while it was investigating war crimes in Ukraine; Dutch intelligence turned him back. In 1975 a Pakistani metallurgist working inside the Dutch side of a uranium-enrichment consortium took its centrifuge designs home, and they later reached Iran, Libya and North Korea. In 1976 a US aircraft maker was found to have paid the prince consort, a senior military figure, to help it win a Dutch fighter-jet order.

For people in the Netherlands this means their personal details can be sold from a police terminal or a court desk, and violence follows the gangs that have bought insiders.

Nigeria.d:
In Nigeria the people reaching into government are mostly after oil and gas. Foreign oil companies, engineering firms and commodity traders have paid officials, often through local agents, for licences, cargoes, construction contracts and favourable legal outcomes, as many have admitted in foreign courts, some for conduct spanning nearly two decades; one engineering consortium admitted paying about $180 million to officials, from the top of government down to the state oil company, to build a gas plant. A US diplomatic cable records a Shell executive saying in 2009 that the company had seconded its own staff to every ministry dealing with oil, which Shell denies. Not every case holds: in 2026 a London jury acquitted a former petroleum minister of taking a life of luxury from businesspeople seeking state oil contracts.

The cost falls on the public treasury: money lost to a bribed contract, an oil block sold through a former minister's company, or an arbitration award obtained by bribing a government lawyer is money that does not reach schools, clinics or roads.

Pressure also comes from inside the country. Confraternities, secretive brotherhoods that began at universities, are hired by politicians for election work, and some have been rewarded with government posts; police in several countries treat the best known, Black Axe, as an organised crime group, even though the constitution bars members of secret societies from elected office. In 2012 the president himself said Boko Haram, the jihadist group, had sympathisers in the army, police and government, naming no one. Voters where confraternities work face intimidation at the polls. The Global Organized Crime Index scores Nigeria high for officials working for criminal interests, with middling courts and watchdogs.

Pakistan.d:
In Pakistan, outsiders reach into the state through business owners close to government, religious and militant movements and foreign spy services. An official inquiry found in 2020 that sugar-mill owners in or allied to the ruling party took a large share of the export subsidies their government granted while sugar prices at home rose about 30 per cent. In 2025 a court convicted former Prime Minister Imran Khan and his wife of taking land for their charitable trust from the property developer Malik Riaz Hussain while their government let £190 million that Britain had sent to Pakistan pay the developer's own court fines; Hussain and Khan's party reject the case.

Religious and militant movements and foreign states have reached into the courts and the army. Under General Zia, members of Jamaat-e-Islami, the main Islamist movement, got judicial jobs and kept his Islamisation agenda going after his death. Militant and Islamist groups have recruited serving officers, up to brigadier, for plans to seize power from inside the army, and officers up to lieutenant-general have been jailed for passing secrets to foreign spy agencies.

The ISI, the military's spy agency, in turn reaches into elected politics. Pakistan's Supreme Court found in 2012 that it had passed bank money to politicians in the 1990 election to stop Benazir Bhutto winning, and in 1989 its officers tried to win over members of her own party so they would vote her out.

For Pakistanis this means export subsidies and money returned from abroad have gone to business owners close to the government that handed them out, the army charged with protecting them has held officers working for movements or foreign services of their own, and at least one election was bought by the state's own spies.

Paraguay.d:
Paraguay's record shows criminal and foreign-linked money reaching the top of government, the Congress and the middle of the justice system. The Global Organized Crime Index gives it one of the highest scores in the world for officials working for criminal interests.

At the top, the reach runs through the Tri-Border Area around Ciudad del Este, where free-zone trade lets goods and money move with little checking and where Hezbollah, the Lebanese armed movement and party, has long had finance networks. The US Treasury sanctioned a former president and a sitting vice-president in 2023, saying their representatives collected bribes at private Hezbollah events in Paraguay; the sanctions on the former president were lifted in 2025 without any court ruling either way.

Below that, cocaine networks moving drugs along the Hidrovía river route and across the Brazilian border keep legislators, prosecutors, police, court staff and prison guards on their side. Prosecutors have charged sitting members of the Chamber of Deputies, mostly from the governing Colorado Party, with getting traffickers released, taking their money for campaigns or laundering it, and Brazil's largest prison gang, the PCC, has paid prison staff on the border to let its members out.

For people in Paraguay this means the police who should investigate traffickers, the prosecutors who should charge them, the courts that should try them and the deputies who write the laws have all had members on the traffickers' side.

Portugal.d:
In Portugal outside interests have reached government mainly through money and the people around the prime minister, and more recently drug networks have reached the customs officers at its ports.

Banco Espírito Santo, run by the Espírito Santo family, had been close to power since the Salazar dictatorship. Its collapse in 2014 wiped out the savings and shares of people who had trusted it, and prosecutors say money from the group reached a former prime minister, José Sócrates, while he was in office; the trial began in 2025 and all defendants are presumed innocent.

In 2023 police investigating a €3.5 billion data-centre project found that its developer had hired a lawyer who was a friend of Prime Minister António Costa, and found €75,800 in envelopes in the office of Costa's chief of staff. Costa, who was not a suspect, resigned and the government fell; a judge later found evidence of influence peddling but dismissed other corruption charges, and all deny wrongdoing.

Portugal is also an entry point for cocaine from Latin America, and police say Brazil's largest crime group, the PCC, and Colombian cartels paid customs officials and port staff at Lisbon, Setúbal and Sines to let several tonnes in; two customs officials were among those detained in 2025. The Global Organized Crime Index scores Portugal in the middle range for officials working for criminal interests and fairly well for its courts and watchdogs. For Portuguese people, money from a bank close to power is alleged to have reached a prime minister in office, a large investor could reach the prime minister's office through his friends, and some of the officials meant to stop drugs at the ports are accused of being paid to let them through.

Rwanda.d:
No documented case yet meets the map's test for Rwanda: none shows a foreign government, crime group, company or movement getting its people or money inside a Rwandan public body and steering what it decided.

The Global Organized Crime Index gives the best available estimate. It scores Rwanda in the middle range both for officials working for criminal or outside interests and for the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs. That places Rwanda neither among the countries where officials are most often bought nor among those where they are least likely to be.

For Rwandans this means the risk that an official is acting for someone else is rated as moderate, and the courts and watchdogs meant to catch such cases are rated as neither strong nor weak.

Saudi Arabia.d:
In Saudi Arabia most of the documented reach runs two ways: foreign arms and aircraft suppliers paying the Saudi officials who buy from them, and Saudi intelligence money going out into foreign banks.

The kingdom is one of the world's largest buyers of weapons and aircraft, and suppliers have paid officials in the state bodies that place the orders. The clearest case is the communications contract for the Saudi Arabian National Guard, the force that protects the royal family: a British company then owned by Airbus held it from 1994, and British prosecutors said about 12 per cent of its revenue went to Saudi officials, including the Guard's then deputy head, to keep contracts worth at least £1.6 billion. The company pleaded guilty, though two executives were acquitted in 2024 after arguing the British government required the payments. A Brazilian aircraft maker also admitted paying an official of a Saudi state company $1.65 million to secure an aircraft purchase.

Outward, Saudi intelligence has gone into foreign finance: Kamal Adham, head of Saudi intelligence until 1979, fronted the secret takeover of a Washington bank by BCCI, a bank later closed worldwide for fraud, and paid a $105 million fine in the United States.

The Global Organized Crime Index gives Saudi Arabia one of the highest scores in the world for officials working for criminal interests. For Saudis, this means a share of the public money spent on defence has gone to the officials and princes who chose the suppliers, the cases have been brought only abroad, and residents have no domestic route to check how state money is spent at home or overseas.

Sierra Leone.d:
Sierra Leone sits on the route that carries South American cocaine to Europe through West Africa, and traffickers using it look for protection inside the state rather than ways around it. They need the people who control an airport or a landing clearance, and the record here shows them reaching both, from ground staff up to the cabinet.

In 2008 a plane carrying about 700 kilograms of cocaine and painted with Red Cross markings landed at Lungi, the international airport, with help from airport and security staff who were later convicted; proceedings indicated that the aviation minister had cleared the landing, and he was dismissed but never tried.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores state-embedded crime here at 8 out of 10 and the strength of courts, police and watchdogs at about 4. For people in Sierra Leone that means the convictions have reached baggage handlers and guards while the minister who cleared the landing was dismissed and never tried, so staff who might be approached by traffickers see the risk falling on those at the bottom rather than on those who gave the orders.

Solomon Islands.d:
In the Solomon Islands foreign governments compete for the loyalty of members of parliament, and the money goes to MPs directly. When the country switched recognition from Taiwan to China in 2019, MPs told reporters that both Beijing and Taipei had offered them hundreds of thousands of dollars for their votes, so the decision on which government to recognise was made by the people both sides were trying to pay.

The offers came on top of an older arrangement. Taiwan used to pay into a discretionary fund run by the prime minister's office, from which payments go to MPs, and China took over that fund after the switch.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores state-embedded crime here at 7.5 out of 10. For voters this means they cannot tell whether their MP's vote on recognition was cast for them or for the government offering the money.

Spain.d:
In Spain, outsiders reach the state mainly through payments for contracts and laws, and along the drug routes on its southern coast. Money from businesses seeking public contracts, permits or favourable laws is the most widespread channel, and it has reached the leadership of both main parties. The courts found that the People's Party itself took part in a contractor's kickback scheme from 1989. In the governing Socialist Party, two successive organisation secretaries, the party's third-ranking post, are accused of taking money from companies seeking public business: José Luis Ábalos, also transport minister, was sentenced in 2026 to 24 years, and the Supreme Court is investigating whether the builder Acciona paid kickbacks through his successor while winning works worth more than €537 million, which he denies. Payments from industrial-gas firms to a former finance minister's consultancy are also alleged to have bought changes to tax law.

Along the Strait of Gibraltar, hashish and cocaine groups pay police, customs officers, dockworkers and airport staff around Algeciras to wave loads through, and the reach goes to Madrid: in 2024 the head of the capital's police unit for money laundering was arrested with €20 million in cash in his home, accused of shielding a cocaine network.

Organised groups have also worked from inside institutions. Before the 1936 coup a clandestine pro-fascist society enrolled almost half of Spain's serving officers, and courts found that ETA, the armed separatist group, used the party Batasuna to hold elected seats and passed the public money paid to them on to its own funds.

For people in Spain, public works, tax rules and permits have been decided by who paid the party in charge, and around Algeciras the police and port staff may be on a trafficker's payroll.

St. Vincent and the Grenadines.d:
Nothing is documented here, so this is an estimate. No case has been found of foreign governments, companies or criminal groups paying or placing officials in St Vincent and the Grenadines.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores state-embedded crime here at 2 out of 10, and the strength of courts, police and watchdogs at about 5.4, near the middle of the scale. The pressure that exists nearby is the cocaine route north from South America through the eastern Caribbean.

For residents, this means there is no known case of an official here acting for an outside paymaster, and the low score suggests the risk is small. The estimate rests on the index's assessment rather than on any inquiry or court ruling in the country, so it describes what conditions suggest, not what has been checked, and a case that has not yet come to light would change it.

Switzerland.d:
Switzerland is where much of the world's governance sits, and much of the infiltration recorded here is aimed at those bodies rather than at the Swiss state. Geneva hosts the World Health Organization, the UN Human Rights Council and the ISO, which sets world technical standards; Zurich hosts FIFA, Lausanne most Olympic sports federations, and Basel the Bank for International Settlements. Outsiders have worked to get inside each. Tobacco companies spent years working through consultants and other UN agencies to weaken the WHO's tobacco work, according to a WHO expert inquiry. Bid committees have allegedly paid FIFA and Olympic voters for hosting rights. When Microsoft wanted its document format approved by the ISO, partner companies joined national committees to vote yes, and Sweden's vote was annulled.

The country's banks and commodity traders are also a channel for reaching other governments. Swiss-based traders have been convicted of bribing officials who hand out oil contracts in Africa and Latin America. The CIA and West Germany's BND secretly owned a Swiss cipher firm, Crypto AG, so the machines it sold to governments let the two agencies read their coded messages.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores state-embedded crime here at 1.5 out of 10. For Swiss residents, this means paying for prosecutors who keep finding the country's banks and traders moving bribes. For people elsewhere, it means that decisions taken in Geneva, Zurich and Lausanne on health rules, technical standards and which country hosts which games can be shaped by whoever got people or money inside first.

Tanzania.d:
In Tanzania the documented reach-in comes mainly from foreign companies selling power, weapons and finance to the state, which have won or kept contracts by paying officials or people close to them. The pattern has repeatedly reached cabinet level. A British arms maker paid its local agent about $12 million, roughly 30 per cent of the price of a $40 million military radar sold in 1999, and the attorney general at the time later resigned as a minister after British investigators found $1 million in his offshore account, though Tanzania's anti-corruption bureau cleared him. A South African bank's local arm paid $6 million to a 'partner' firm with a government official among its directors while raising $600 million for the state, and $122 million from a power-company escrow account was moved to a private power producer whose associate had paid a minister.

Other outside ties sit closer to the ruling party. Since 2022 a leadership school in Kibaha, paid for by China's Communist Party, has trained officials from Tanzania's ruling party and five others in southern Africa, openly and with government agreement.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials working for criminal interests here at 6 out of 10 and courts and watchdogs at about 4.2. For Tanzanians, this means electricity, defence and borrowing have repeatedly cost them more because officials took a share, foreign donors held back almost $500 million in budget support over one scandal, and in most cases no one in Tanzania has been convicted of taking the money.

Tonga.d:
No case is documented of a foreign state, company or criminal group paying or placing officials inside Tonga's government, so this is an estimate based on conditions.

Tonga is a small kingdom where, until reforms in 2008, the monarch held most day-to-day power, and decisions about the country's money could be made by the king and a few advisers. The Global Organized Crime Index places Tonga in its Moderate band, scoring officials acting for criminal interests at 6 out of 10. That score suggests outside money could reach some officials, most likely through public contracts, licences or decisions made by a small circle around the government.

For people in Tonga this means there is no named official, company or group acting for an outside interest that they can point to or hold to account. The estimate rests on the index's assessment rather than on any inquiry or court ruling, and a documented case would change it.

Turkmenistan.d:
Turkmenistan is one of the most closed states on Earth: there is no independent press, no opposition party and no court that rules against the government, and almost nothing about how the state works is made public. The one documented case of outsiders reaching in comes from a foreign court record about companies selling to the government. To keep its vehicle sales to the Turkmen state, the German carmaker Daimler gave a high-level official an armoured Mercedes worth about $300,000 as a birthday present in 2000, paid about $250,000 to translate and print 10,000 German copies of the Ruhnama, the spiritual guide written by President Saparmurat Niyazov, and made other payments to officials. Daimler settled the US case in 2010.

No case shows a foreign state or criminal group placing people inside the government. The Global Organized Crime Index puts Turkmenistan in its severe band, scoring officials acting for criminal interests at 9 out of 10, among the highest in the world, and the strength of courts, police and watchdogs at 2.2, among the lowest.

For people in Turkmenistan this means that foreign companies seeking state orders have learned to pay officials and flatter the president's personality cult, and the cost is carried in public spending they cannot see. No journalist, judge or auditor in the country can find out whether officials act for outside interests, and the only account of this case came from prosecutors abroad.

United Arab Emirates.d:
The United Arab Emirates uses its state companies to place its own people at the head of international bodies. In 2023 the chief executive of ADNOC, the state oil company, presided over the UN's COP28 climate talks, and leaked briefing papers showed his team preparing to raise oil and gas business in meetings with foreign governments.

The UAE is also a place where outside crime reaches others' governments. Dubai's free-zone companies, whose owners can stay hidden behind a required local sponsor, have been used by foreign drug organisations to employ the men who work for them, including one that prosecutors say paid politicians and a security chief in Bosnia. At home, the government has made the accusation the other way: in the 2013 'UAE 94' trial the attorney general said members of Islah, an Islamist group, had tried to infiltrate ministries, schools and universities as part of a plot against the government.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal interests in the UAE at 6.5 out of 10. For people elsewhere, this means a UN climate summit was chaired by the head of a state oil company preparing oil deals, and crime groups can use Dubai companies to employ the people who pay officials in their own countries.

Uzbekistan.d:
In Uzbekistan, foreign companies entered one of the country's most valuable markets by paying the president's family. Three foreign telecom groups, VimpelCom, Telia and MTS, paid companies controlled by Gulnara Karimova, elder daughter of then-President Islam Karimov, to obtain mobile licences and radio frequencies; Uzbek prosecutors put her kickbacks at $869 million, and the three firms later paid about $2.6 billion between them to settle foreign bribery cases. Karimova has been convicted twice in Uzbekistan and remains in prison.

The pattern shows how access to a closed economy worked: under Karimov, a foreign investor did not compete in an open tender but paid a gatekeeper close to the ruler. The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal interests in Uzbekistan at 7 out of 10 and the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs at 3.8, so the conditions that made such deals possible have not gone away.

For people in Uzbekistan, this meant paying for a mobile service whose licences were sold privately to the president's daughter instead of to the operator offering the best terms. Most of the settlement money went to the governments of the United States, the Netherlands and Sweden, not to Uzbekistan, and weak courts leave citizens with little means to find out whether officials are making similar arrangements today.

Vietnam.d:
In Vietnam, the documented pattern is businesses and criminal networks buying the officials who are meant to regulate, police or buy from them, from provincial party chiefs up to ministers and the central bank.

The largest case is in banking. A property tycoon secretly controlled one of the country's commercial banks for a decade through more than two dozen nominee shareholders, used it to take about US$12.5 billion in loans for her own companies, and paid the head of the central bank's inspection department $5.2 million to keep it off the watch list; she was sentenced to death in 2024.

Most cases are about public money. Construction, property and medical-equipment companies have paid provincial party secretaries, provincial chairmen and project boards to rig tenders for roads, bridges and hospital supplies. During the pandemic one company bribed health officials across the country to buy its overpriced Covid tests, and businesses paid officials in three ministries to approve the repatriation flights that were the only way home for Vietnamese abroad, then raised ticket prices to recover the cost. Foreign firms work the same way: the US chemicals company Albemarle paid more than $218 million to settle US charges that its agents bribed officials at state refineries. Police drug teams have been charged with shielding a Laos–Vietnam trafficking network.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal interests at 7 out of 10 and the strength of courts, police and watchdogs at 4.8. For people in Vietnam this means bank savings, hospital budgets, road contracts and even a seat on a flight home have been for sale to whoever paid the official in charge, and an ordinary courier caught with drugs can be executed while the officers who protected the network are tried in the same courts.

Albania.d:
Albania lies on a main route by which cannabis and other drugs move from the Balkans across the Adriatic into Italy and the rest of the EU, and the groups on that route work on both sides. To keep that trade running they reach into the institutions meant to stop it, through family and political ties at the top and payments to police, prosecutors and judges lower down. Businessmen reach city government the same way.

At the top, Italian police arrested a cousin of the interior minister, the minister in charge of Albania's police, in a probe into an Albanian-Italian cannabis group, and wiretaps in that probe mentioned the minister; he was convicted only of abuse of office, so no court has said whether the group had him working for it.

Lower down, messages from Sky ECC, an encrypted phone service read by European police, have given SPAK, Albania's special anti-corruption prosecutor, evidence that crime groups had senior police officers, a prosecutor and members of the judiciary working with them. The same prosecutor has sent the mayor of Tirana, the capital, to trial on charges that four businessmen gave him and his wife more than €1 million in benefits while he approved construction permits and moved city funds to companies tied to her; he denies it.

As an EU candidate, Albania is judged partly on how its courts handle these ties. The Global Organized Crime Index scores Albania 6.5 out of 10 for officials working for criminal interests and about 5 for the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs. For people living there, the officer investigating a killing or the prosecutor deciding whether to charge may be taking instructions from the group responsible, and a building permit in the capital may have gone to whoever paid the mayor's family.

Antigua and Barbuda.d:
Antigua and Barbuda is a small state with a small civil service, and the documented cases show outsiders with far more money than its government reaching the one official whose signature they needed.

Agents working for Colombia's Medellín Cartel ordered Israeli military weapons in Antigua's name, with forged papers, to arm the forces of a cartel leader. An Israeli diplomatic note said the guns were shipped at the apparent instruction of the minister Vere Bird Jr, son of the prime minister, and after Colombia complained an official inquiry recommended he be barred from public office for life. The island's business as an offshore financial centre, where foreign-run banks take deposits from around the world under Antiguan licences, created the second opening. R. Allen Stanford ran Stanford International Bank from Antigua and was later convicted in the United States of a $7 billion fraud; the head of the Antiguan regulator meant to supervise his bank took cash, private-jet flights and sports tickets from him, left the bank's real assets unexamined and told US investigators his office had no power to help them.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores the country 3 out of 10 for officials working for criminal interests and about 4.7 out of 10 for the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs. For people living there, both cases meant outsiders used the state's name and licences for their own business: Antigua's name went on a cartel's arms order, and thousands of savers, on the island and abroad, lost their money in a bank that the regulator had been paid not to look at. In both cases the facts came out through pressure from abroad, from Colombia and from US prosecutors, rather than from Antigua's own institutions.

Austria.d:
Austria sits between east and west, and Vienna has long been a base for foreign spy services. The documented reach-in runs mostly from Russia, into Austria's own security state and into the international bodies headquartered here, and the record shows it lasting decades rather than being a recent turn. An Austrian army colonel passed military secrets to the GRU, Russia's military intelligence, from 1992 until 2018 in return for about €280,000, and was convicted in 2020.

The same reach has since appeared inside Austria's domestic intelligence agency. A former officer was convicted in 2026 of working for Russia through Jan Marsalek, the fugitive former Wirecard executive: he used police databases to find people Moscow was looking for, including a journalist, and handed over work phones from the interior minister's office. He plans to appeal. Russian money has also reached sport: an independent inquiry found that the president of the International Biathlon Union, based in Salzburg, took Russian cash, hunting trips and favours over many years and in return shielded Russian athletes from doping action.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Austria 4 out of 10 for officials working for criminal or outside interests and about 7.5 for its courts, police and watchdogs. For exiles, journalists and others Russia's government wants to find, the risk is that an official with access to state databases may be working for a foreign service, which turns the state's own records into a way of locating them. For Austrians generally, it means officers in the army and the intelligence service have worked for a foreign power while holding the secrets the country shares with its EU partners, and the cases have come to light years after the leaks began.

Bangladesh.d:
In Bangladesh outsiders have reached public institutions from three directions: business groups taking over banks, an Islamist movement reaching into the army, and party networks filling the universities.

The banks are where the most money has moved. Under Sheikh Hasina's government, which fell in August 2024, conglomerates close to it drew on ordinary people's deposits. From 2017 the S. Alam Group took control of Islami Bank Bangladesh and several other Islamic banks, installing its own chairman, board and managers beyond the legal limits, and it is reported to have drawn huge loans from them.

A coup attempt by serving and retired army officers, which the army says it stopped in 2012, was linked to Hizb ut-Tahrir, a banned movement seeking a single Islamic state. Since 2024 the interim government has filled the universities from the networks of the BNP and the Islamist Jamaat-e-Islami, taking names from the BNP leadership: 30 of 47 new vice-chancellors had close ties to their teachers' groups.

For depositors, the bank holding their savings may have been run for the group that took it over. Soldiers have been drawn into a plot to seize power on behalf of a movement outside the state, and students and staff have seen university leadership handed to the networks of the parties now close to government.

Belize.d:
No case of an outside party placing people or money inside Belize's government or companies remains on this map after checking. That is a statement about the documented record, not proof that none exists.

Belize sits between Mexico and Guatemala on the Caribbean coast, on routes used to move cocaine north from South America, and it offers offshore company registration. Those are the conditions under which outside money tends to look for officials willing to help. The Global Organized Crime Index scores Belize 5.5 out of 10 for officials working for criminal or outside interests, in the middle of the range, but only about 3.6 out of 10 for resilience, meaning the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs, which is weak.

For people living there, this means there is no documented case in which they can name an official acting for an outside party. The weak resilience score matters more: if traffickers or foreign buyers did reach officials, the courts, police and regulators that should catch it are rated as poorly placed to do so. The records that would show it first are the ownership of registered companies and how drug cases on the coast and the border are handled.

Bosnia and Herzegovina.d:
Bosnia and Herzegovina sits on the Balkan route by which cocaine and other drugs reach western Europe, and Balkan cocaine networks with bosses abroad use the country to move and clean their money.
