The documented pattern today is those networks paying Bosnian officials to help: in 2024 police in Sarajevo arrested 23 people for trafficking and laundering money for the inner circle of a cocaine boss already sentenced in the Netherlands, and Europol, the EU police agency, said those detained included corrupt officials who had worked for the group. The case is at the charging stage.

Outsiders have found a way into the security services before. During and just after the 1992–95 war, Iran, one of Bosnia's few wartime allies, built a presence inside the Interior Ministry; in 1996 NATO-led troops raided a training site where Iranians worked alongside Bosnian ministry staff, and the United States made shutting down the intelligence agency close to Iran a condition of its military aid.

The divided government left by the 1995 peace deal gives outsiders room. Power is split between the Federation and the Serb-run Republika Srpska, each with its own police and ministries, and between ethnic parties within them, so there are many separate offices to approach. The Global Organized Crime Index scores Bosnia 8 out of 10 for officials working for criminal interests, among the highest in Europe, and about 3.9 out of 10 for the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs, among the lowest.

For people living there, this means an official handling their permit, case or complaint may also be working for a criminal network whose leaders live abroad, and the bodies that should catch that are rated among the weakest on the continent.

Bulgaria.d:
Bulgaria sits on the Balkan route, the main land route by which drugs and smuggled goods enter the European Union, and smugglers get through it by paying the customs officers and border police who are supposed to stop them. When the United States sanctioned Bulgarian officials and business figures for shielding smuggling networks in 2021, it was the largest anti-corruption action of its kind Washington had taken against any single country, and several of those named held customs and border posts.

The same sanctions reached the top of the state. The US Treasury said Delyan Peevski, a member of parliament and media owner, used bribes and influence to control key institutions; in 2013 parliament had made him head of the national security agency and he quit a day later only because thousands protested. The courts are a further target, with claims under investigation that compromising files on judges and prosecutors have been used to steer their decisions.

Russia's military intelligence, the GRU, has reached inside the defence establishment of this NATO member. Prosecutors charged a ring in 2021 that included a senior defence ministry official, two serving military intelligence officers and the former head of parliament's registry of classified information, accused of passing NATO and EU documents to the Russian embassy; they remain on trial.

For people living here, this means goods crossing the border without the checks the law requires, a security service whose leadership has been open to the people it should watch, and allied secrets held by officials who may have been working for Moscow. The Global Organized Crime Index rates Bulgaria high for officials working for criminal interests and its institutions only middling. Few of those named abroad have been charged at home.

Cambodia.d:
No documented case in Cambodia yet meets the map's test, which asks for an outside party that got its people, money or control inside a government body or company and had decisions there serve it. This entry is an estimate.

The Global Organized Crime Index rates Cambodia among the worst countries in the world for officials working for criminal interests, with weak courts, police and watchdogs to push back. Scam compounds, fenced sites where trafficked workers are held in debt bondage and forced to run online fraud, operate in the open, and US and British sanctions have named political protection as the reason. On the Index's scores it is likely that criminal money reaches officials, but the record so far shows owners close to power rather than decisions shown to have been taken inside the state for them. Cambodian courts have prosecuted none of the people sanctioned abroad.

Chad.d:
In Chad outside money reaches in at two levels: foreign companies seeking oil rights go to the presidency, and drug traffickers go to the security services. At the top, the clearest case is a Chinese energy company: an envoy working for CEFC China Energy, which promoted China's Belt and Road programme, offered President Idriss Déby a $2 million bribe, dressed up as a donation, to win oil rights, and was convicted for it in New York in 2018. The company's chairman denied authorising him.

Lower down, tramadol, a prescription painkiller, is trafficked illegally across the Sahel, and the network moving it through Chad counted high-ranking army and intelligence officials among its members. Analysts who read the court papers when ten members were convicted in 2020 described large sums circulating among them, some used in attempts to bribe judges and the security services.

When army and intelligence officers are inside a trafficking network, Chadians depend for protection on police and courts that the same network has tried to buy, and when oil rights are offered to the president for cash, decisions about the country's main resource are made for the payer. The 2020 conviction shows Chad's courts can act, but the Global Organized Crime Index rates Chad among the countries where officials most often work for criminal interests, and its courts, police and watchdogs among the weakest.

Déby, president from 1990 to 2021, was also named as a Freemason in press reports, alongside several other presidents of former French colonies in Central Africa. Freemasonry is a fraternal society whose members meet privately in lodges and swear oaths of mutual support. No lodge was named for him, and no decision of his is tied to it.

Comoros.d:
Comoros, a small island state off East Africa, has been reached by outsiders through the men around its president and through its officials. For about eleven years from 1978, its presidential guard was commanded by Bob Denard, a French mercenary who worked for France's secret services: he led the coup that returned President Ahmed Abdallah to power, then ran the force meant to protect him while building up business interests and Comorian citizenship. When Abdallah ordered the guard disarmed in 1989 he was shot dead shortly afterwards, and Denard led another coup in 1995 that French troops ended; the court that later tried him recognised the secret services' role.

The more recent documented reach comes from a tobacco company. Leaked records from British American Tobacco (BAT) show the company arranging bribes for Comorian officials, part of a run of payments in several African countries that included efforts to block tobacco-control laws based on the World Health Organization's tobacco treaty. A British fraud inquiry closed without charges and BAT denies wrongdoing.

For Comorians, this means that for a decade the armed men around their head of state answered to a foreigner tied to another country's spy service, and if the tobacco payments worked as reported, they now live under weaker limits on tobacco sales and advertising than the treaty sets. The Global Organized Crime Index rates Comoros high for officials working for criminal interests, with very weak courts, police and watchdogs.

Cote d'Ivoire.d:
The documented outside reach in Côte d'Ivoire is an international lender placing its own official at the head of the economy.

In 1990 the International Monetary Fund pressed President Félix Houphouët-Boigny to put Alassane Ouattara, who had directed the IMF's African Department, in charge of economic policy; he became prime minister that November while the IMF's programme was still running, later returned to the IMF as its deputy head, and has been president since 2011. For Ivorians this meant that the man running their economy during an IMF programme came from the lender setting its conditions, and the decisions on spending and prices taken under that programme were made by the lender's own former official.

The Global Organized Crime Index rates Côte d'Ivoire high for officials working for criminal interests, with courts, police and watchdogs of middling strength. No documented case on the map shows a criminal group paying Ivorian officials.

Czech Republic.d:
The documented outside reach into the Czech state comes from two sides: Russian intelligence, and a lobbyist's network inside public companies. Russia's foreign intelligence service, the SVR, has worked the old way, by recruiting insiders: in 2022 the government confirmed that a long-serving Foreign Ministry employee with top-secret clearance, who had worked at headquarters and in embassies, had repeatedly taken its money for diplomatic information. He was removed, but prosecution was thought unlikely because intelligence material cannot be used in Czech courts. Prague has also been a base for Russian money aimed at legislatures elsewhere: in 2024 the government exposed Voice of Europe, a Russian-funded website that Czech intelligence says passed money to sitting and aspiring European legislators.

At home, police say a group around Michal Redl, a Zlín businessman and lobbyist linked to the STAN party, steered contracts and money at Prague's city-owned transport company, which runs the metro, trams and buses, through a deputy mayor and senior managers of the firm, to benefit businessmen connected to the group, and reached contracts at the state health insurer as well. Thirteen people were charged in 2022, the education minister resigned over his contacts with Redl, and the trial is under way, with the main accused denying guilt.

For Czechs, this means a diplomatic service in which a foreign spy agency was able to pay a cleared official for years, with no trial to show what he passed on, and a city transport company whose contracts, prosecutors say, were decided for a lobbyist's friends rather than for the people who ride it. The Global Organized Crime Index rates Czech officials low to middling for working with criminal interests, with relatively strong institutions.

Dominican Republic.d:
In the Dominican Republic outside money has reached officials through public works contracts and, far more often, through the drug trade. Odebrecht, the Brazilian construction company, admitted paying $92 million in bribes in the country to win public works, and a former public works minister was convicted over it.

The Dominican Republic is a transit point for cocaine bound for Puerto Rico, the United States and Europe, and traffickers buy protection at every level that can touch a shipment. They have recruited officers of the National Drug Control Agency to guard loads, navy officers in charge of port security, army colonels who leaked arrest warrants and raid plans, and intelligence and interior officials who gave a fugitive trafficker a state identity card and gun permits. The reach goes into Congress and the agencies: a congressman and a state agency head were among one cocaine network's contacts, and the congressman tried to help a man avoid extradition. A convicted trafficker says his money paid for a presidential campaign, a claim never tested in court. Since 2009 the drug agency has removed hundreds of staff and the national police has expelled well over a thousand officers.

For Dominicans, public works were paid for under contracts that carried tens of millions of dollars in bribes, and the officers, legislators and officials meant to stop the drug trade have included people working for it, so a raid can be known to the target before it happens. The Global Organized Crime Index rates the country in the middle range for officials working for criminal interests, with weak courts, police and watchdogs.

Equatorial Guinea.d:
Equatorial Guinea is a small oil and gas producer on the Gulf of Guinea, ruled by Teodoro Obiang since 1979, and the record of outsiders reaching into its government runs almost entirely through oil. The foreign companies that produce and trade its oil have paid the president, his family and the officials who award contracts. A 2004 US Senate inquiry found that American oil companies producing most of the country's offshore oil made payments to Obiang, his relatives and officials for land, office leases, security and scholarships for officials' children, and that Obiang and his family held secret shares in their joint ventures with the government. Later, the Dutch company SBM Offshore admitted that between 2008 and 2012 its local agents passed money on to at least nine officials of the oil ministry and the state oil company, and a Swiss-based commodity trader has pleaded guilty in Britain to bribing officials in five African oil states, this one among them.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal or outside interests at 9 out of 10, among the highest anywhere, and the courts, police and watchdogs that would resist them at just over 2. That combination describes a state where the people in office control the main source of money and no independent body can question how contracts are given out.

For Equatoguineans, this means oil revenue that could pay for services has been shared between foreign companies and the ruling family, with officials' children educated abroad on company money. With one president in power for more than four decades and weak courts, they have no domestic route to find out who was paid; every documented case was brought by investigators abroad.

Ethiopia.d:
No documented case in Ethiopia yet meets this map's test of an outside party getting its people, money or control inside the government and steering it. The prime minister's membership of a Pentecostal church is lawful, and no record shows the church directing government decisions.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal or outside interests at 6 out of 10 and the courts and watchdogs at 4.5, which suggests more is going on than has been documented. Civil war in Tigray and continuing conflict in Amhara and Oromia make reporting on officials harder, and the weak watchdogs mean there is little official scrutiny of how decisions are made. The shading here is an estimate from those scores.

Gabon.d:
No documented case in Gabon yet meets the map's test, which asks whether an outside party got its people, money or control inside a government body, international body or company, and whether decisions there served it.

The best available estimate comes from the Global Organized Crime Index. It scores officials acting for outside or criminal interests in Gabon at 7.5 out of 10, and the courts and watchdogs that should catch them at 3.5. Taken together, these scores point to a state where officials can serve outside interests with little risk of being exposed, so the lack of a documented case may partly reflect how little is investigated.

For people in Gabon this means there is no independent record to show whether the officials who govern them answer to someone else.

Ghana.d:
In Ghana the documented case of an outside party getting inside the state comes from the drug trade. Cocaine moves through West Africa on its way to Europe and the United States, and the traffickers who move it need officials who will look away or help.

In 2006 a large cocaine load landed from a ship and then disappeared. Traffickers were secretly taped meeting the police director of operations at his home about their missing drugs. An inquiry found the police account unsatisfactory and recommended that he be prosecuted, but he returned to duty.

For Ghanaians this means traffickers have reached a senior post in the police, the body meant to stop them, and the officer at the centre of the lost cocaine kept his job. The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal interests at 7.5 out of 10 and courts and watchdogs at about 5.3.

Guinea.d:
Guinea holds one of the world's largest untapped iron ore deposits, at Simandou, and the documented cases of outside interests getting inside its government are about who controls it. Both sides of the long fight over the deposit are recorded as paying, or trying to pay, people at the top of the state.

In 2008 the government took two blocks of Simandou from the mining company Rio Tinto and gave them to a company controlled by Israeli businessman Beny Steinmetz; a Swiss court later found that he got them by bribing a wife of President Lansana Conté, which he denies. Rio Tinto, trying to keep its own rights, hired a French banker who was a close friend of a former senior Guinean official, and US regulators found that, acting for the company, he offered at least $822,000 to a Guinean government official; Rio Tinto paid a $15 million penalty without admitting or denying the findings.

In both cases the way to national resources ran through payments to people close to power rather than through open bidding. For Guineans, that meant control of one of the world's largest iron deposits was fought over through the president's household and his officials, and years of potential state revenue were lost while the rights were contested. The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal or outside interests at 8 out of 10 and the courts and watchdogs at under 3, so cases like these tend to be pursued abroad, if at all.

Honduras.d:
Honduras is one of the main stopping points for cocaine flown and shipped from South America towards Mexico and the United States, and over the past two decades trafficking groups bought protection at the very top of the state. According to US courts, traffickers paid a president, his brother in Congress and a national police chief to let cocaine through, and trial evidence said drug money paid for the governing National Party's election campaigns. The clearest single case is Juan Orlando Hernández, president from 2014 to 2022, who was convicted in New York of protecting cocaine shipments and pardoned by the US in 2025.

The arrangement worked from the bottom up as well as the top down. On the Guatemalan border, a cocaine trafficker became mayor of his own town and paid into the ruling party's presidential campaign in return for national protection. US prosecutors have also named a former president as a recipient of traffickers' money, based on cooperating witnesses; he has never been charged. The Cachiros, a Honduran trafficking clan, laundered money through a bank owned by one of the country's most powerful political families, which regulators closed after the US sanctioned it.

For Hondurans, this means mayors, police, Congress and the presidency have all been used to move cocaine, and the governing party's campaigns were paid for with drug money, according to US trial evidence. The main cases were tried abroad, and the former president was released, so Hondurans have not seen these officials tried at home. The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal interests at 8.5 out of 10 and courts and watchdogs at under 4.

Indonesia.d:
In Indonesia outside forces reach the state mainly through money, business and religious movements. Under Suharto, a Muslim intellectuals' association headed by the minister Habibie moved its members into the civil service and ministries and used that place to set up religious courts and an Islamic bank. Armed Islamists have tried the same route: officials say Jemaah Islamiyah, the network behind the 2002 Bali bombings, tried for over a decade to get its people into the military, police and ministries, and one of its advisers sat on the fatwa commission of the state-recognised Ulema Council, which issues religious rulings.

Business helps write the law and decide how it is applied. When the government drafted its 2020 omnibus jobs law, which rewrote dozens of laws on labour, land and permits, it put the chairman of the national chamber of commerce in charge of the consultation. Firms have paid the people who buy from them, judge them or guard state assets: aircraft makers paid the head of the state airline, contractors paid the Speaker of parliament, illegal gambling sites paid communications ministry staff to stay off its block list, and prosecutors say palm-oil groups' lawyers paid judges to acquit them. At PT Timah, the state tin company, directors let private smelters mine its concessions under a disguised leasing deal, at a cost put at about 300 trillion rupiah, mostly environmental damage.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Indonesian officials 8 out of 10 for working for criminal interests. For Indonesians this means the rules on their wages and land were drafted with employers at the head of the table, the Bangka Belitung islands were dug up by smelters who had the state firm's directors on side, and a court verdict or a website block can depend on who has paid.

Israel.d:
In Israel the outside party with the deepest reach into the state is the settler movement, which builds settlements in the occupied West Bank and has long drawn state money to outposts the government's own rules forbade. One of the movement's leaders runs the civil administration that decides on land and building in the West Bank. After the 7 October 2023 attack the movement also came to sit inside the army there: thousands of settlers called up as reservists serve in local defence units staffed largely by residents of the settlements they guard, and the army has dismissed dozens for violations including attacks on Palestinians.

The ultra-Orthodox parties take their decisions from councils of senior rabbis, who used their place in government to protect seminary students' exemption from military service and in 2025 ordered their ministers out after the Supreme Court told the army to start drafting them.

Prosecutors say Benjamin Netanyahu, as communications minister, gave valuable decisions to a telecoms owner in return for favourable coverage, which he denies; a former head of his bureau and a former minister are charged with taking bribes from the Israeli agent of a German shipbuilder whose submarines the state was buying. Iranian intelligence recruits Israelis online, including soldiers in the Iron Dome missile-defence system, and 35 such espionage cases had been made public by the end of 2025.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Israel 5.5 out of 10 both for officials serving outside interests and for its courts and watchdogs. For Palestinians in the West Bank, the official deciding whether their homes stand comes from the movement that wants their land, and the soldiers posted near their villages are often settlers from the settlements nearby. For Israelis, who serves in the army has been set partly in rabbis' councils.

Jordan.d:
In Jordan, outside forces have reached the state through its rulers, its border guards and its parliament. For about twenty years, until 1977, the CIA made secret yearly payments of millions of dollars to King Hussein; President Carter stopped them just before The Washington Post reported them. Today's pressure comes from drug smugglers on the Syrian border. Smugglers moving captagon, an amphetamine pill made in Syria, need the border to stay open to them, so they recruit the people guarding it, and serving and former soldiers have been convicted of carrying pills and weapons across.

The Muslim Brotherhood, a Sunni Islamist movement that works to bring its members into power, competed openly through its own party, the Islamic Action Front, which became the largest party in parliament in the 2024 election. In 2025 the government banned all of the Brotherhood's activities and said it would seize its assets, after arrests over an alleged weapons plot that the group said it knew nothing about.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Jordan 6 out of 10 for officials working for criminal interests and above 5 for its courts and watchdogs. For families in northern Jordan this means living on a smuggling route where some of the soldiers paid to stop the drugs have been caught moving them. For the voters who made the Islamic Action Front the largest party, it means their party's parent movement is now banned and its members face arrest.

Korea, DPR.d:
In North Korea the state itself is the organisation that crosses borders, and the one documented case on this map runs the other way: the government reaching into an international body rather than an outside force reaching into it. In the Pyongyang office of the UN Development Programme, the UN's main aid agency, most local staff were nominees chosen by the government against UN policy, their salaries were paid to the state in hard currency, officials had to be present at project visits, and the government moved its own funds abroad through a UN account. A 2008 US Senate inquiry set this out, and the UN suspended its programme there in 2007 after the government refused new controls.

The Global Organized Crime Index gives North Korea the worst possible score, 10 out of 10, for officials taking part in criminal activity, and one of the lowest anywhere for its courts and watchdogs. The US Justice Department has charged networks that placed thousands of North Korean IT workers, using stolen or fake identities, in remote jobs at foreign companies, with their wages paid into accounts controlled by the state.

For people in North Korea this means that aid meant for them passes through staff picked by the government, and money from work done abroad in their name goes to the state rather than to them. With no independent courts, press or watchdogs, they have no means of learning how the aid or the earnings are spent, or of challenging it at home.

Kyrgyzstan.d:
In Kyrgyzstan criminal networks have reached into the state through the customs service, the office that decides what crosses the border and what duty is paid on it. A smuggling operation with people inside customs controls both what comes in unchecked and how much revenue the state loses. The clearest case is Raiymbek Matraimov, a deputy head of customs whom journalists tied to a scheme that moved hundreds of millions of dollars out of the country, and whom the US sanctioned in 2020; at home he settled by repaying money and served no prison term at the time.

The state has been harder on those who expose these links than on the officials named: journalists from the organised-crime reporting network OCCRP and the Kyrgyz outlet Kloop, who documented the customs scheme, were prosecuted or forced out, while the official they wrote about stayed free.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Kyrgyzstan 8.5 out of 10 for officials working for criminal interests and below 4 for the strength of its courts and watchdogs. For people in Kyrgyzstan this means customs revenue that should have paid for schools, roads and hospitals has left the country, the officials at the centre of it face little at home, and the reporters who tell them about it pay a higher price than the officials do.

Lesotho.d:
Lesotho's largest public project is the Lesotho Highlands Water Project, a World Bank-backed scheme of dams and tunnels that sells the country's water to South Africa, and it is where foreign companies reached in. Engineering and construction firms from abroad working on the scheme paid Masupha Sole, chief executive of the state authority that ran it, through intermediaries, and Swiss bank records later showed millions of maloti he could not explain. In 2002 Lesotho's own High Court convicted him of bribery and jailed him for 15 years after appeal, and it went on to convict a Canadian engineering firm and a German consultancy; the World Bank barred the Canadian firm from its contracts for three years.

That case is unusual because a small, poor country prosecuted the foreign companies itself. No later case of a foreign state, company, crime group or lodge placing people inside the government remains on this map. The Sovereign Military Order of Malta, a Catholic order with diplomatic status, has a documented presence, but nothing ties it to any decision. The Global Organized Crime Index scores Lesotho 7 out of 10 for officials working for criminal interests and below 4 for the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs, which suggests the thin record reflects thin reporting more than an absence of influence.

For people in Lesotho this means the scheme that sells their main natural resource was run for years by an official taking money from the firms building it, and they pay for that kind of arrangement through inflated contracts and lost public money. Today the risk is greatest in contracts, licences and policing that ordinary residents cannot easily question.

Lithuania.d:
Lithuania has faced two kinds of reach-in: the intelligence services of Russia and Belarus recruiting people inside its armed forces, volunteer defence units and security services, and money from business reaching politicians and their parties. In both, its own courts have done the catching.

Russia's military intelligence, the GRU, and its security service, the FSB, have repeatedly tried to buy people with access. A GRU agent working as a military surgeon recruited an air force officer at the base that hosts NATO's Baltic air patrols for documents and officers' files, and an FSB officer was caught in 2015 trying to recruit members of the presidential guard to plant listening devices. Belarus's military intelligence has used the same method since 2022: two Lithuanians recruited on a trip to Minsk gathered information on the armed forces and NATO equipment, and one joined the Riflemen's Union, the volunteer defence organisation linked to the army, in order to spy.

On the money side, the clearest case is the president removed in 2004: a Russian helicopter businessman who had funded his campaign was then granted citizenship by presidential decree, and parliament impeached him, the first European head of state removed that way. Domestic business buys in too: in 2024 the Supreme Court made final the convictions of the Liberal Movement's leader, a Labour MP and an executive of one of the largest business groups for bribes paid to get decisions through parliament.

The Global Organized Crime Index rates Lithuania's institutions as fairly strong and finds a moderate level of officials serving criminal interests. For Lithuanians this means the soldiers, volunteers and guards protecting them and the members of parliament voting on their laws have each been targets for payment, but when it has come to light, their own courts have convicted those involved.

Malaysia.d:
In Malaysia outside money and networks have reached the state at the top, at its borders and on the street. Goldman Sachs bankers paid bribes to officials in Malaysia and Abu Dhabi to win the bond business of 1MDB, a state investment fund, and billions were then stolen; Najib Razak, prime minister until 2018, was convicted over more than $1 billion found in his own accounts. His successor, Muhyiddin Yassin, is on trial accused of using his office to help firms win contracts under a Covid-era public works programme while they paid money to his party, which he denies.

Foreign states have used Malaysian companies as cover. North Korea's spy agency secretly controlled Malaysian firms that fronted for its military radio business.

Lower down, criminal syndicates keep officers on their side. Traffickers moving methamphetamine from the Golden Triangle pay narcotics officers to release suspects and put seized drugs back on sale, and the anti-corruption commission has prosecuted such officers repeatedly, mostly in Johor and the Klang Valley around Kuala Lumpur. Phone-scam syndicates do the same: in 2021 the national police chief said 34 members of the force were suspected of working for a single 'Macau scam' gang. At Kuala Lumpur's main airport, agents bringing in foreigners pay immigration officers to wave their clients through without proper checks.

For Malaysians, a public fund meant to pay for development filled a prime minister's accounts and left the country with the debt, people in Johor and the Klang Valley live where some of the officers paid to stop drugs have sold them back onto the street, victims of phone fraud have reported it to a force some of whose officers were working for the fraudsters, and the officers deciding who enters the country have been paid by the people bringing them in.

Marshall Islands.d:
The documented outside reach into the Marshall Islands is an attempt by foreign businesspeople to buy a law that would have given them their own territory. Two China-born businesspeople paid members of parliament and other officials over several years to pass a law creating a semi-autonomous 'special administrative region' on Rongelap Atoll. Both pleaded guilty in the United States, and the US government later barred a former Marshallese president and an MP from entering the country for taking the bribes; the former president denies it.

The scheme shows how a small Pacific state can be approached. A parliament of a few dozen members meant that paying a handful of lawmakers could move a law. The Global Organized Crime Index finds a relatively low level of officials serving outside interests in the Marshall Islands, which fits a country where this was a single scheme rather than a settled arrangement.

For the people of Rongelap this means lawmakers were paid to put their home under a separate set of rules written for the buyers. No one has been charged in the Marshall Islands, so the case was settled in a foreign court, and Marshallese have no ruling of their own on which officials took money.

Micronesia.d:
What is documented for the Federated States of Micronesia is an accusation made by its own head of state. In 2023, shortly before leaving office, President David Panuelo wrote a long letter saying China was using bribery and threats against Micronesian officials as 'political warfare', with the aim of keeping the Pacific country on Beijing's side, or neutral, if war broke out over Taiwan. He wrote that he had considered switching diplomatic recognition from China to Taiwan. China rejected the claims, no court or inquiry has tested them, and no official has been named as taking money.

The method described is one suited to a small state: a government of a few dozen senior officials decides which of China or Taiwan it recognises and how it votes abroad, so paying or pressing a handful of them can move the whole country's foreign policy. What China would gain, if the account is true, is a Pacific government that stays friendly or neutral in a war over Taiwan. The Global Organized Crime Index finds a relatively low level of officials serving outside interests in Micronesia.

For Micronesians, if the president's account is true, some of their officials have made decisions on foreign policy and security after taking money or giving way to threats from abroad. Because nothing has been investigated, they cannot tell which officials, if any, were involved, or whether later choices about Taiwan and defence were made freely.

Montenegro.d:
In Montenegro, organised crime has had protectors at the top of the state for three decades. In the 1990s, when cigarettes were smuggled from Montenegro across the Adriatic to Italy, Italian anti-mafia prosecutors charged that the state itself protected the trade and indicted the country's leader, Milo Djukanovic, in 2008; immunity kept him from trial, and he went on to lead Montenegro until 2023.

Today the trade is cocaine, and the protection has reached the justice system. Montenegrin clans such as the Kavac clan have needed judges, prosecutors and police chiefs who will look away or tip them off, and messages from Sky ECC, a cracked encrypted phone service used by criminals, have exposed how far this went. Since Europol, the EU's police agency, passed those messages to Montenegro, former heads of the Supreme Court, the special prosecution office and the police have been charged with protecting crime groups. The clearest case is the former Supreme Court president convicted in 2026 of using her position to shield a smuggling network run by her son.

Foreign governments have tried to reach in too. Prosecutors accused two Russian military intelligence officers of plotting with pro-Russian opposition MPs to seize parliament in 2016 and stop Montenegro joining NATO; a first court convicted them, but a retrial acquitted everyone.

The Global Organized Crime Index finds officials in Montenegro widely serving criminal interests. For people there this means that the judges, prosecutors and police chiefs they would turn to were, in several cases, working for the groups they were meant to pursue, and anyone whose case reached the Supreme Court in those years cannot be sure it was heard fairly. Most of these charges are still unproven, and the evidence came from foreign police and prosecutors rather than from Montenegro's own institutions.

Namibia.d:
In Namibia, the documented outside reach is through the country's natural resources, where a foreign company is alleged to have bought access from the ministers who control it. Namibia's fish belong to the public, and the government hands out quotas, licences to catch a set amount. In the case known as 'Fishrot', leaked files published in 2019 showed that Samherji, one of Iceland's largest fishing companies, had paid people close to the government to obtain horse-mackerel quotas. The fisheries and justice ministers resigned and were arrested with several associates, and they face racketeering, corruption and money-laundering charges under Namibia's organised crime law. Samherji denies paying bribes, and no one has yet been convicted.

The mechanism is one seen wherever a few ministers control who may take a public resource such as fish, timber or minerals: a foreign company that pays those ministers or their associates can be given a share that would otherwise go to local firms or be sold for the public's benefit. The Global Organized Crime Index finds a moderate-to-high level of officials serving outside interests in Namibia and rates its institutions as fairly weak.

For Namibians, if the charges are proved, two ministers sold a public resource to a foreign company. Local fishing firms and their workers lost quota they would otherwise have had, and the state lost income that would have gone to the public budget. The trial has run for years, so people still wait for a court to say who took part.

New Zealand.d:
In New Zealand the documented reach inside government comes from two directions: the Chinese state, which has had people in Parliament whose ties to it were known to the intelligence services but not to voters, and drug networks, which police say have paid prison staff.

The clearest example of the first is Jian Yang, a National MP who had been a Communist Party member and had taught at Chinese army schools that trained intelligence linguists. New Zealand media reported that the agencies had raised concerns about his relationship with the Chinese government; the matter was settled quietly between party leaders, and he and a second MP left Parliament at an election. The case rests on those media reports rather than an official finding.

Organised crime has generally had little hold on officials, and the Global Organized Crime Index gives New Zealand one of the world's lowest scores on that measure. The exception now before the courts is in Auckland's prisons, where police allege that prisoners coordinating drug imports from their cells had staff take cash to bring in phones and drugs. In 2026 police charged fifteen prison staff: ten Corrections officers and five employed by Serco, the private company that runs one of the jails.

For New Zealanders, this means they elected MPs whose links to a foreign government were known to the security services and not to them, and learned of it through the press, and that some of the officers paid to keep prisons closed to the outside may have been working for the people held inside them.

North Macedonia.d:
In North Macedonia outsiders have reached into politics and the justice system by paying or directing individual office-holders, most visibly around the 2018 agreement that renamed the country so it could join NATO, which Russia opposed. Interior ministry documents seen by investigative reporters say Ivan Savvidis, a Russian-Greek billionaire and former member of Russia's parliament for the ruling party, paid at least €300,000, some carried across the Greek border in cash, to more than a dozen politicians from several parties, nationalist groups and football hooligans ahead of protests in which a petrol bomb was thrown at parliament; he denied funding the protests. Leaked counter-intelligence files from 2017 say a Serbian intelligence officer at Serbia's embassy gave instructions to an MP in the ruling coalition and that Russian intelligence officers tried to recruit army and interior ministry staff.

The justice system has been bought from inside as well. The Special Prosecution Office, set up to pursue high-level crime after a wiretapping scandal, was compromised when a television personality close to its head sold the country's richest man milder treatment in his case; in 2020 a court jailed him for bribing her and jailed her for misuse of office. Separately, the foreign minister joined the World Economic Forum's Young Global Leaders network in 2025, which is lawful and shows no decision taken for it.

The Global Organized Crime Index gives North Macedonia a fairly high score for officials working for criminal or outside interests and middling strength in its courts and watchdogs. For people in North Macedonia this means a decision about their country's name and alliances was contested with foreign money paid to their own politicians, and the office created to prosecute the powerful was itself for sale.

Palau.d:
Palau's documented case shows how a criminal group can reach a small state's government through the front door of business and goodwill. In Pacific island states, organised crime groups from Macau and Hong Kong arrive as investors and cultural associations, ask local officials to sit on their boards, and propose casinos or special economic zones that would sit partly outside national law.

The clearest example is Wan Kuok-koi, known as 'Broken Tooth', a former head of Macau's 14K triad whom the US Treasury sanctioned in 2020. Immigration records reported by OCCRP, a network of investigative journalists, show he was listed as a 'guest of the government' on a visit in 2018–19, and a serving postmaster general and a state governor became directors of his Palau association, which planned a casino zone on Angaur island where he would control customs, ports and an airport. It stopped in 2019 when the president, warned by Taiwan of Wan's record, came out against it, and the association applied to dissolve. OCCRP did not establish that the Chinese state directed the effort, and no one in Palau has been charged.

For a country of about 18,000 people, two serving officials lending their names gave a sanctioned gang leader local standing, and one island came close to hosting a casino zone under his control. What stopped it was a presidential decision on a foreign government's warning, not a law that blocked it.

Peru.d:
In Peru, money from builders has reached the presidency and the transport ministry, and criminal networks have bought people inside the offices that keep the country's records, grant its pardons, guard its ports and store its weapons.

Public works are where the money has gone deepest. Odebrecht, the Brazilian construction group, paid former president Toledo about $35 million for the contract to build the Interoceanic Highway, and he has been sentenced over it. Peruvian firms have done the same at home: prosecutors say a cartel of construction companies paid officials of the transport ministry and its roads agency so that 30 public works went to its members, four of the firms have admitted it, and in 2025 another former president, Martín Vizcarra, was convicted of taking money from two builders while he was a regional governor; he is appealing.

Lower down, criminals buy the officials who handle paperwork, sentences, inspections and stores. Staff of the national property registry rewrote the recorded owners of disputed land, the board that advised the president on pardons sold early release to convicted drug traffickers, cocaine groups pay security staff, dockworkers and customs contacts at Callao, and an army lieutenant is accused of taking rifle ammunition out of a Lima fort for Ecuadorian gangs. Judges and the council that appointed them have been recorded on wiretaps trading rulings and promotions. The Global Organized Crime Index scores Peru high for officials working for criminal interests.

For Peruvians this means they have paid for roads, irrigation and hospitals awarded in return for bribes, a land title can be changed by whoever paid the registrar, a trafficker can buy his way out of prison, and someone going before a court cannot be sure the outcome was not arranged.

Qatar.d:
Qatar's documented cases run in two directions: foreign arms makers paying the officials who buy for its armed forces, and Qatar's own money reported to have reached inside another country's government.

The clearest case is in arms buying. The US Justice Department found that Raytheon, the American missile maker now part of RTX, paid at least $2 million from 2012 to 2016 through sham contracts with a company owned by the official who ran procurement for the Qatar Emiri Air Force, and won additions to an air-defence contract in return; RTX agreed in 2024 to pay a $252 million criminal penalty for the bribery. Going the other way, Israeli prosecutors are investigating aides of the Israeli prime minister over money reported to have come from Qatar to promote its image from inside his office.

Qatar's residents have no elected body able to ask how state money is spent, whether on weapons at home or on influence abroad, and the air-force case came to light only through a US prosecution. The Global Organized Crime Index scores Qatar fairly high for officials working for criminal or outside interests.

Samoa.d:
No case of outside groups paying or placing officials in Samoa is documented yet, so this account is an estimate based on general conditions. The only outside organisation recorded as present is Shincheonji Church of Jesus, a South Korean religious movement, and its presence is lawful and not evidence of wrongdoing.

The Global Organized Crime Index places Samoa in its low band, scoring it low for officials working for criminal or outside interests and in the middle range for the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs. Neighbouring Pacific states have seen bribes for business deals, and small island governments with few investigators are the kind of place where such pressures can go unnoticed.

For residents, the absence of cases means there is no specific harm to point to, not that none exists. The bodies that would bring such cases to light, the courts, police and audit office, are the ones whose middling scores leave that question open.

Senegal.d:
In Senegal the one documented claim of an outside group getting inside the state concerns a drug ring and the police. In 2013 the country's anti-drug chief accused his predecessor, by then national police chief, of having worked with a drug ring while he ran the anti-drug office. The police chief was removed, but an inquiry found no evidence, and the claim remains contested.

It does not show a pattern, and no other case on the map shows a foreign state, crime group or company getting its people or money inside a Senegalese public body.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Senegal in the middle range both for officials working for criminal interests and for the strength of its courts and watchdogs. For Senegalese, this means the officials they deal with are rated as neither often nor rarely acting for criminal interests, and the one serious accusation against a police chief was investigated and not upheld.

Singapore.d:
Singapore appears on the map mainly as a base from which other governments are reached. For years a Singapore ship-supply firm run by Leonard Francis bribed US Navy officers with cash, travel and gifts for ship schedules and inside information, while a civilian Navy contracting officer in Singapore stopped an early inquiry; US prosecutors charged 33 people.

At home, the government treats foreign influence, most often linked to China, as something that works through ordinary community life: business chambers, clan and grassroots associations and universities. Its response is to name the people it believes are being used, and it does this by ministerial decision, not by trial. Since 2024 a foreign-interference law lets it designate residents, so far a business-chamber leader who had attended a Chinese Communist Party united front body, and make them report each year their political donations and foreign ties.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores state-embedded crime here at 1.5 out of 10, among the lowest in the world, and courts and watchdogs at about 7.8. For residents this means the bribery on record ran through a local firm into a foreign navy rather than into their own government, while people who lead community or business groups with ties to China can be publicly named and made to disclose their links without the evidence being tested in court.

Somalia.d:
In Somalia the outside force reaching furthest into the state is al-Shabaab, the al-Qaeda-linked armed Islamist group fighting the federal government, which places its own people inside the government it is trying to overthrow. Its members take public jobs, sometimes under false names, to collect information for taxing businesses and choosing targets, and defectors are often taken into the security forces without vetting. In 2019 a woman working under a false name in the Mogadishu mayor's office blew herself up at a meeting there, killing the mayor and other officials. In 2023 the national intelligence agency said it had arrested ten al-Shabaab spies inside government agencies in Mogadishu, after an attack on an army training centre that killed at least 25 trainees appeared to have had inside help, and opposition parties have urged the president to purge the agency itself of the group's operatives. The government has also dissolved a Chamber of Commerce board after finding the group's representatives on it.

Alongside the state's tax system the group runs its own, which a UN panel of experts described as 'mafia-style' taxation at Mogadishu's port and markets. Foreign states compete for influence at the top as well: from 2019 to 2021 the intelligence agency was run by a former reporter for Qatar's state-funded Al Jazeera, whom Somali media and analysts accuse of channelling Qatari money and interests into government, which Qatar denies.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores state-embedded crime here at 8 out of 10 and the strength of courts, police and watchdogs at about 1.9, among the weakest anywhere. For people in Somalia that means paying tax twice, to the government and to the group fighting it, and working in offices or training in army camps where a colleague may be passing on who should be taxed or killed.

Sri Lanka.d:
In Sri Lanka two kinds of outside force are documented inside the state: organised crime, which has bought officers in the army and police, and a Buddhist nationalist movement, whose leader was given a hand in writing the law.

The crime side came to light in 2025, when the gang leader Kehelbaddara Padme was returned from Indonesia with four associates. Investigators say his network had people across the security forces: an army lieutenant colonel and a colonel were detained over allegedly selling firearms and rifle ammunition to the gang, a police sub-inspector in a crime investigation unit was arrested over close ties to Padme, and a former local councillor is accused of running drug and arms operations on his orders. The public security minister said police and immigration officials helped the gang obtain forged passports.

The second case is in lawmaking. In 2021 President Gotabaya Rajapaksa put Gnanasara, leader of Bodu Bala Sena ('Buddhist Power Force'), a monks' group accused of stirring violence against Muslims, in charge of a task force to draft a single legal code for the country. Drafting law is the work of Parliament and the Justice Ministry, and the Bar Association said the task force was taking that work over.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores state-embedded crime here at 7 out of 10 and the strength of courts, police and watchdogs at about 3.7. For people in Sri Lanka this means guns sold by army officers and passports obtained with officials' help can reach a gang, and for Muslims and other minorities, that the law meant to govern them was being drafted by a cleric whose group was accused of violence against them, through a body that bypassed the elected parliament.

Sudan.d:
In Sudan armed and political movements have repeatedly taken over the state from inside. The longest-running is the Islamist movement derived from the Muslim Brotherhood. Led by Hassan al-Turabi, it spent the decade after he became attorney general in 1979 placing members in high posts, took power through army officers in 1989, and under Omar al-Bashir filled state jobs with its own people. A committee set up after Bashir fell in 2019 began removing them, but after the army's coup of 2021 a special court reinstated scores of officials in the central bank, the judiciary, the prosecution service and the foreign ministry.

Since the war between the army and the Rapid Support Forces paramilitary began in 2023, the Islamists have gone back inside the army itself. Military sources said thousands of men from Bashir's former intelligence service, with ties to the movement, joined the army, the US says one Islamist brigade has supplied more than 20,000 fighters, and the army chief relies on Islamist backing.

Armed Darfur movements entered by another door: a 2020 peace deal gave them about a quarter of the cabinet, and one rebel leader has run the finance ministry since 2021, staffing it with his movement's members.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores state-embedded crime here at 8.5 out of 10 and courts, police and watchdogs at about 2.3. For people in Sudan, this means the courts, the central bank and the ministries that handle their money are staffed by the appointees of movements rather than chosen for the job, officials removed for their party ties can be put back by a court after a coup, and the army fighting the war is partly run by a movement that the US says has obstructed a ceasefire.

Syria.d:
Syria's state was taken over in the 1960s by a closed group that built its own structure first. The Military Committee, a secret body of army officers formed in 1958 and hidden even from their own Ba'ath party's leaders, used army units to carry out the 1963 coup and held the real power inside the new government. One of its founders, Hafez al-Assad, seized power in 1970, and he and his son Bashar ruled until December 2024.

That ruling circle was itself reached from outside. By 1965 Israel's Mossad had planted an agent, Eli Cohen, under a false identity among Syria's leaders, where he heard officials discuss army plans and reported them to Israel.

The Global Organized Crime Index gave Assad's Syria 10 out of 10 for state-embedded crime and about 2 for courts and watchdogs. For people in Syria, this meant decades of rule by a group that had organised in secret inside the army, with police and courts that answered to it rather than to them, and no independent court or elected body able to hold it to account.

Thailand.d:
In Thailand criminal businesses reach into the state mainly through the police, who have been accused of selling protection to gambling, drug and visa rackets. In 2023 the deputy national police chief was removed and investigated over alleged protection of an online gambling network, a case that split the police leadership in public.

Chinese crime groups working in Thailand have used the same route. In a crackdown that began in late 2022, investigators charged at least 80 immigration police, three of them generals, with demanding bribes over visas issued to about 5,000 Chinese nationals, which let them stay and run illegal businesses; police suspect one club in Pattaya is a triad base. A Chinese businessman accused of drug and money-laundering crimes had gained Thai citizenship by marrying a senior police officer, and she and five other officers were dismissed over links to his case.

Organised groups outside the elected system have also long decided who holds power. In 1932 the People's Party, founded by Siamese students in Paris, ended absolute monarchy with army units, and its members held the prime ministership for about two decades; the army's habit of taking power by coup dates from that event.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores state-embedded crime here at 7 out of 10 and courts and watchdogs at about 5. For people in Thailand this means the officers who decide on a visa or a complaint may be working for the businesses involved, and residents cannot be sure which reports to the police will be followed up.

Trinidad and Tobago.d:
In Trinidad and Tobago the documented reach-in has come through people holding public posts while serving outside interests: contractors on the country's largest public works, an international sports body, and now armed gangs. The clearest case is the new terminal at Piarco International Airport, built in the late 1990s: contractors, led by a Miami engineering firm, worked with the then finance minister to rig bids and charge inflated prices. In 2023 a Miami jury found the former minister and two businessmen liable for racketeering and fraud, awarding the country US$131.3 million. Jack Warner, meanwhile, was a vice-president of FIFA, world football's governing body, while he served as works minister and then national security minister until 2013; US prosecutors later charged him with taking bribes in his football roles, charges never tried because Trinidad's High Court blocked his extradition in 2025.

The gangs reach in through the prisons. When the government declared a state of emergency in July 2025 over a plot, hatched by jailed gang leaders, to kill public officials, it detained a prison superintendent it said had used his post to get contraband to the plotters and support the gangs' leaders inside.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores both officials acting for criminal interests and the strength of courts, police and watchdogs at about 5 out of 10. For people in Trinidad and Tobago this means the airport they paid for cost far more than it should have because their finance minister was working with the contractors, that the minister once responsible for their police was also an officer of a body later accused of selling votes, and that gang leaders the state has locked up can still plan killings with help from the officers guarding them.

Tuvalu.d:
No case of outside groups paying or placing officials in Tuvalu is documented, so this account is an estimate based on conditions. Tuvalu is a nation of about 11,000 people on low-lying atolls, and its government depends heavily on foreign aid and on agreements with larger partners. Elsewhere in the Pacific, payments for business deals have drawn smaller states into larger powers' rivalries; none of this is documented in Tuvalu.

The Global Organized Crime Index places Tuvalu in its Minimal band, scoring officials acting for criminal interests at 1.5 out of 10 and courts, police and watchdogs at 5.9. For Tuvaluans this means there is no known current harm from hidden outside influence. The risk is that a country this small has only a handful of officials, auditors and police, so if an outside interest did reach in, there would be few people in a position to notice it.

United Kingdom.d:
In Britain outsiders reach in four ways: foreign intelligence services recruiting people inside the state, fraternities placing members in office, companies getting inside the departments that regulate them, and crime groups buying staff at the ports. Soviet intelligence had agents inside MI6, MI5 and the Foreign Office in the mid-20th century; today China and Iran are the most active. MI5 says a solicitor working covertly with China's United Front gave donations to an MP whose office employed her son, and in 2026 a Hong Kong trade office manager and a Border Force officer he directed were convicted of spying on dissidents.

In Northern Ireland every prime minister from 1921 to 1969 belonged to the Orange Order, a Protestant fraternity, and a 1973 army estimate put up to 15% of a local regiment in loyalist paramilitary groups, some of whom took part in killings of Catholics. In England, Freemasons inside the police have been described steering a top appointment and taking a detective off an inquiry that pointed to the lodges.

Firms have paid MPs to lobby for them, the big accountants lend tax staff to the Treasury to help draft law they then advise on, and a Conservative peer pushed her husband's firm through the pandemic 'VIP lane' for contracts. At the ports, cocaine importers recruit port security guards and Border Force officers, who run customs and passport checks, to let their vans and couriers through.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials serving criminal interests at 3 out of 10 and courts at 7.6. For people in Britain, this means rules drafted or enforced by those they apply to, drugs passing checkpoints staffed by people a gang has recruited, and, in Northern Ireland, families still seeking inquiries into killings in which soldiers and police took part.

Vanuatu.d:
No case of outside groups placing people inside Vanuatu's government or paying its officials is documented, so this account is an estimate based on general conditions.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal interests in Vanuatu at 3 out of 10, a low score, but scores its courts, police and watchdogs at only 4.9, in the middle of the range. That means experts judge that officials are not often working for criminal or outside interests, but that the bodies meant to catch it if they were are only moderately able to do so.

For ni-Vanuatu, as the country's people are called, the absence of cases means there is no named official or company to hold to account, not proof that none exists. With courts and watchdogs in the middle of the range, it would take time for any hidden outside influence on officials to come to light.

Yemen.d:
Yemen's case on the map is a neighbouring government paying Yemen's own leaders. A Saudi government body, the 'Special Committee', kept about 2,700 Yemeni political, tribal and military leaders on monthly pay, as records from 2012 show, and directed named sheikhs and a serving brigade commander, so people holding Yemeni office and command were also answering to Riyadh.

Yemen has been at war since 2014, and its state has split. In the north, the Houthi movement, a Zaydi Shia armed group, took over the capital Sanaa and its state institutions in 2014–15 and still rules most of Yemen's population through its own council. In the south, the internationally recognised state is run by the commanders of the forces fighting the Houthis, several of them backed by Saudi Arabia or the UAE.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Yemen's courts, police and watchdogs at 1.9 out of 10 and officials acting for criminal interests at 8. For Yemenis, this means the sheikhs and commanders who decide local matters may be paid by a foreign government, and there is no court or police force they can turn to when an armed group takes their land or money.

Algeria.d:
In Algeria the documented reach-in comes from two directions: foreign firms paying officials for state contracts, and the cocaine trade buying protection inside the security state. Contractors have worked on the public works ministry and Sonatrach, the state oil and gas company, through agents. The clearest example is the East-West motorway, begun in 2006 by Japanese and Chinese consortia: in 2015 an Algiers court jailed an adviser to the Chinese group, a former director of highways and other ministry staff over kickbacks on the project, whose cost rose from $6 billion to at least $13 billion. Bribery charges brought in Italy against a foreign oil-services firm over Sonatrach contracts ended in acquittal, but Algeria's energy minister from 1999 to 2010 was later sentenced in absentia to 20 years for corruption.

The cocaine trade reached into the police. When 701 kilograms of cocaine were found at the port of Oran in 2018, hidden in a cargo of imported meat, press reports tied the importer to judges, prosecutors, mayors and the children of senior politicians. The seizure brought down the head of the national police, and he and several generals were later convicted of corruption and illicit enrichment rather than drug offences; Algeria has published little about who protected the shipments.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Algeria 7.5 out of 10 for officials working for criminal interests and about 4 out of 10 for the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs. For Algerians, this means public money for roads and energy has passed through officials who took a share, while the officials who let cocaine through a state port have not been named in court, and residents cannot tell whether they are still in post.

Argentina.d:
Argentina's state has more than once been run from inside by secret circles. Officers' lodges made and unmade the first governments after 1812 and, by most historians' account, organised the 1943 coup that began Juan Perón's rise. In the 1970s P2, a secret Masonic lodge run from Italy, counted an interim president, ministers, a junta member and generals among its members, and they gave the lodge's grand master a diplomatic post and a place as an adviser inside the state.

Since the 1990s the route has run more through business and money. In 1991 a team of economists trained in a business-funded think tank took over the economy ministry and ran its own programme there, which ended in frozen savings and the 2001 collapse. People close to those in power have drawn on state business under governments of left and right: in 2025 a judge charged former president Alberto Fernández over a decree that sent all state bodies' insurance through one state insurer, on which a broker married to his private secretary earned nearly 60 per cent of the commissions. Under the current government, drug distributors are accused of paying kickbacks inside the national disability agency; the accused deny it.

Crime reaches the police and the courts, above all in Santa Fe province around Rosario, where drug and gambling bosses have had a provincial police chief, detectives who warned them of raids and the city's chief prosecutor on their side. Federal judges, who hear drug cases, have been convicted of selling traffickers release or house arrest. For people around Rosario, the detective, prosecutor or judge who should stand between them and the gangs may be on the gangs' side. Nationally, public money for insurance and disabled people's medicines has been steered to people close to those spending it.

Azerbaijan.d:
Azerbaijan's economy rests on oil and gas, and the state oil company, SOCAR, is closely bound up with the government. Outsiders have tried to get in by sharing the oil wealth with the officials who control it: in the late 1990s foreign investors trying to buy SOCAR in a privatisation they expected to be rigged made senior Azerbaijani officials their secret partners, promising them two-thirds of the profits.

Since then the oil sector and Azerbaijani money have reached outward, into international bodies that set rules for them. When Azerbaijan hosted the UN climate summit, COP29, in 2024, its president had been a SOCAR vice-president, and its chief executive was secretly filmed discussing oil and gas deals with campaigners posing as investors. An inquiry for the Council of Europe's parliamentary assembly, Europe's human rights body, reported in 2018 a strong suspicion that some members had acted for Azerbaijan in return for money or gifts, known as caviar diplomacy.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Azerbaijan 8.5 out of 10 for officials working for criminal or outside interests and about 4 for its courts, police and watchdogs. For people living there, oil wealth that belongs to the country has been treated as something officials could share privately with foreign buyers, and the European bodies meant to report on their rights have been targets of their government's money. For people elsewhere whose coasts and harvests depend on emissions falling, the talks that decide how fast oil and gas are phased out were chaired by people from the industry that sells them.

Barbados.d:
Barbados has one documented case of an outside party reaching into its government, and it came from a company seeking state business rather than from organised crime or a foreign state. Senior executives of the Insurance Corporation of Barbados Limited paid the island's Minister of Industry, Donville Inniss, about $36,000 in 2015 and 2016 to help the company win two government insurance contracts covering more than $100 million of state property. The money went through a US bank account in the name of a friend's dental company in New York, which is why a US jury, not a Barbadian court, convicted him of money laundering in 2020; he was sentenced to two years in prison.

No other case of a foreign government, company, crime group or lodge placing people or money inside the state remains on this map. The Global Organized Crime Index gives Barbados 3 out of 10 for officials working for criminal or outside interests, low by world standards, and about 6.1 out of 10 for the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs, better than most of the Caribbean. Barbados is also an offshore financial centre that registers international companies, the kind of business that can draw outside money.

For Barbadians, this means a minister used his office to steer the insurance of public property to a company that paid him, and the case came to light only because the money passed through the United States. The likeliest places for outside money to reach in are the ones this case shows: who wins public contracts, who funds politicians and who owns the companies registered on the island.

Benin.d:
Nothing is documented yet for Benin, so this is an estimate based on conditions. No case found so far shows a foreign state, company, criminal group or lodge paying or placing people inside its government. Two French Masonic bodies, the Grand Orient de France and the Grande Loge Nationale Française, are thought to have members in Benin but are not documented.

Benin is a coastal West African state whose port at Cotonou handles goods for its larger neighbour, Nigeria, and for landlocked states to the north, so much of the trade that crosses it belongs to outsiders. The Global Organized Crime Index scores Benin 6 out of 10 for officials working for criminal or outside interests and about 3.8 out of 10 for resilience, meaning the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs. That combination describes officials under real pressure and weak checks on them.

For people living there, this means that if outside interests are paying or placing officials, it is likely to show up in port and customs work, public contracts and policing, and residents would pay through lost public revenue and weaker protection. With no named case, there is no official or company they can yet challenge.

Botswana.d:
Nothing is documented yet for Botswana, so this is an estimate based on conditions. No case found so far shows a foreign state, company, criminal group, church or lodge paying or placing people inside its government, and no outside organisation is recorded as present.

Botswana's economy rests on diamonds, mined mainly through a long-standing partnership between the government and the De Beers company, and on that kind of single, valuable export outside interests often seek influence. Against that, the Global Organized Crime Index scores Botswana 4.5 out of 10 for officials working for criminal or outside interests and about 5.4 out of 10 for resilience, meaning the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs. That puts it in the middle of the range and ahead of most of its neighbours. The lack of cases may also reflect limited investigative reporting.

For people living there, this means there is no named official or company to hold to account, and no evidence that public decisions are being bought. If a case exists, it would most likely surface through mining and other licences, public contracts or policing of the borders, and those are the records residents would need to see.

Burkina Faso.d:
No documented case in Burkina Faso yet meets the map's test, which asks for an outside party that got its people, money or control inside a government body or company and had decisions there serve it. This entry is an estimate.

The Global Organized Crime Index rates Burkina Faso high for officials working for criminal interests, and very weak in the courts, police and watchdogs that would check them. On those scores, a criminal group or foreign interest trying to place people inside the state, or to buy officials already there, would meet little resistance at home, and the record of it would be thin. The country has been under military government since 2022, and nothing here reaches into that government.

Cameroon.d:
No documented case in Cameroon yet meets the map's test, which asks for an outside party that got its people, money or control inside a government body or company and had decisions there serve it. This entry is an estimate.

The Global Organized Crime Index rates Cameroon among the countries where officials most often work for criminal interests, and rates its courts, police and watchdogs as weak. On those scores, an outside group that paid officials or placed its own people in a ministry or state company would be unlikely to be traced by Cameroon's own institutions, and any such case would more likely come to light through reporting or courts abroad. Paul Biya has held the presidency since 1982, so an inquiry would also have to start from inside a government that has not changed hands in that time.

Chile.d:
In Chile, outsiders have reached the state through three routes: foreign intelligence money during the Cold War, companies paying the officials who write laws, collect taxes and decide court cases, and crime groups buying the officers who police them.

Between 1963 and 1973 the CIA spent about $13 million on Chilean parties, candidates and a newspaper, and under General Pinochet it kept the head of the secret police as a paid contact.

Since the return to democracy the money has come mostly from companies, and it has reached each branch of the state. A holding group used employees inside the tax service to help pass campaign money through fake invoices, and a lawyer's business clients had bribes paid to officials of the tax service and the Treasury, some of whom have since been convicted. A fishing company paid a senator, later jailed for bribery, who voted its way on the 2012 fisheries law that handed a large share of the national catch to companies controlled by a few families. In 2026 a Supreme Court justice was detained, accused of taking money from a Belarusian-Chilean mining-truck consortium over a ruling in which her chamber ordered Codelco, the state copper company, to pay the consortium $20 million rather than the reverse.

As Chile has become a drug transit route, the buying has reached the police and prisons: national police officers have been charged with reselling seized drugs and protecting dealers, and in 2025 about a tenth of the guards at Santiago's main remand prison were charged with smuggling drugs and phones to gangs held there. For Chileans this means laws, tax checks and court rulings that can be bought by the firms they concern, and in some places officers who work for the groups they guard.

Congo, Dem. Rep..d:
For nearly thirty years the armies of Congo's neighbours, and the armed groups they back, have placed their own people inside the Congolese state. After a Rwandan-backed rebellion brought Laurent-Désiré Kabila to power in 1997, a Rwandan officer served as chief of staff of Congo's army; Later a rebel group was folded into Congo's army.

The clearest case today is M23, a rebel force that took the eastern cities of Goma and Bukavu in early 2025. UN sanctions monitors report that Rwanda's army commands it and that it has appointed governors and put Rwandans in charge of mining, tax, banking and border control; Rwanda denies directing M23. Kinshasa says the reach goes to the top of its own state: a military court sentenced Joseph Kabila, president until 2019, to death in absentia in 2025 for working with Rwanda and M23, and the general who commanded the army across the east is on trial for treason over alleged contact with Rwanda. Both deny it, and reports from the general's trial say the prosecution has struggled to prove the contact.

Elsewhere the reach comes through mining, where foreign commodity traders have paid money meant for Congolese officials to win mining and trading business, and one of the largest miners has paid $180 million to settle bribery claims it denies.

For people in the east, the governors, tax collectors and border officers over them have more than once been appointed by a foreign army or a group it backs, and they cannot be sure their own commanders are loyal. Across Congo, mining wealth that should have reached the state budget went to insiders, and the Global Organized Crime Index rates Congo among the worst in the world for officials working for criminal interests.

Croatia.d:
Croatia's documented cases show companies reaching the state through the people at the top of government, to win control of national assets or public money. The clearest is the national oil company, INA. MOL, a Hungarian oil company in which the Hungarian state has influence, wanted to run it, and Croatian courts found that Prime Minister Ivo Sanader took a 10 million euro bribe from MOL's chief executive to give it that control. MOL denies the bribe, and Hungary has not handed the executive over to Croatia.

The pattern continues in health. In 2024 the health minister was arrested and sacked, accused of taking bribes from a group selling medical equipment to approve hospital purchases at inflated prices; prosecutors say tenders were fixed at least four times, two hospital directors are among those charged, and the minister denies it.

For Croatians, the national oil company they part-own is still managed by the firm the courts found paid their prime minister for that control, and hospitals may have paid more for equipment because the minister in charge was paid by the sellers, money that would otherwise have gone on patients.
