In Georgia, criminal and armed groups reached inside the state in the years after independence from the Soviet Union in 1991, Russia has kept trying to recruit people inside its armed forces, and the newest case reaches the security service itself. In the early 1990s a militia, the Mkhedrioni, was made the country's interior forces and was accused of extortion and drug smuggling until it was outlawed in 1995. Alongside it worked the 'thieves in law', a criminal fraternity born in Soviet prison camps, which 1990s governments treated as part of the power structure, according to Georgian analysts and former officials. Membership became a crime in 2005, but in late 2025 and early 2026 police still arrested more than 100 people in a crackdown on it.

Russia's military intelligence, the GRU, has worked from inside Georgia's forces: two years after the 2008 war, Georgia arrested air force pilots and a naval radio operator accused of telling Russia its codes and how ready its forces were. More recently, scam call centres, which phone people abroad and talk them into fake investments, have operated from Tbilisi, one of them near the State Security Service's headquarters. In December 2025 prosecutors charged the service's chief from 2020 to 2025, a ruling-party member, with taking about $1.4 million in bribes, partly in exchange for protecting call centres.

For Georgians this means armed men accused of extortion were once the state's own interior forces, the army defending them against a neighbour that occupies part of their land has had that neighbour's informants in its ranks, and the agency meant to protect them is accused of having been paid to protect fraudsters. The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal interests at 4 out of 10 and courts and watchdogs at 5.

Grenada.d:
Grenada has given ambassador titles to foreign businessmen, and the documented allegations here come from foreign investors dealing directly with the prime minister's office. In 2019 an Al Jazeera investigation reported that one foreign investor said he had paid about half a million dollars to Prime Minister Keith Mitchell, who said he received only $15,000 to cover travel. A US businessman said a partner had been offered a diplomatic post in return for kickbacks on state projects, which the government denies. No charge has been brought, and the claims rest on the investors' own statements.

For Grenadians, this means public contracts and diplomatic posts can be traded with foreign investors, and only the government's word stands between residents and that trade. If a kickback was asked for, it raised the cost of work done for the public. With no court test, residents are left with conflicting accounts. The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal interests at 3.5 out of 10 and the courts and watchdogs at about 5.2, better than most of the region.

Guyana.d:
Guyana produces gold in its interior and has become a route for cocaine moving from South America by air and sea, and the people in both trades pay officials to keep their business moving. According to the US Treasury, the largest gold trading family in the country bribed customs officials to leave more than 10,000 kilograms of gold off customs declarations, paid officials for help in court matters and to win state contracts, and was helped by the top civil servant at the home affairs ministry, who took cash and gifts for contracts, gun permits and passports. The family denies wrongdoing.

Cocaine networks reach the police in the same way. In 2025 the Treasury sanctioned a serving police officer it says arranged safe passage for Mexican and Venezuelan traffickers, along with trafficking bosses and Colombians managing hidden jungle airstrips. None of these cases has been tried, and the US State Department calls corruption in Guyana a significant obstacle to stopping drugs.

Outside interests choosing who governs is older than the drug trade. Before independence the CIA secretly paid opposition parties to remove the elected premier Cheddi Jagan, and kept funding their leader Forbes Burnham, who became the first prime minister of independent Guyana in 1966.

For Guyanese, this means the customs officer, court official or ministry clerk they deal with for a permit or passport may have been paid by a large private business, and duty lost on undeclared gold, more than $50 million by the Treasury's count, was public money. People in the interior live near airstrips used for cocaine, policed by a force that traffickers have reached. The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal interests at 8 out of 10 and the courts and watchdogs at about 4.3.

Iceland.d:
No documented case in Iceland yet meets the map's test, which asks whether an outside party got its people, money or control inside a government body, international body or company, and whether decisions there served it. No case shows a foreign government, a company or a crime group placing people or money inside the Icelandic state.

The Global Organized Crime Index puts Iceland among the lowest anywhere for officials working for criminal interests and near the top for the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs. On that estimate, an official serving outside interests would be both unusual and likely to be caught.

For Icelanders this means they are unlikely to meet an official quietly serving a foreign state or a crime group, and if one were found, the courts and watchdogs are well placed to examine it.

Iraq.d:
Since 2003 Iran's reach has been written into the Iraqi state, from the security forces to the cabinet and now the town halls. Badr, a militia formed in Iran in 1982, held the Interior Ministry, which runs the police. The Popular Mobilization Forces (PMF), about 67 mostly Shia militias almost all backed by Iran's Revolutionary Guards, were made a branch of the armed forces by a 2016 law and are paid from the state budget; their own chief of staff has said they take orders from Iran's supreme leader. The PMF has its own state company to win public contracts, and Iran-aligned armed groups hold ministries, including Badr and Kataib Hezbollah nominees in the cabinet formed in May 2026.

The militias also use their state seats and state-paid units to take over local government. The political arm of one PMF brigade won all four provincial council seats reserved for Christians by mobilising mostly Shia Arab voters, then used its majority on the Nineveh council to remove 15 mayors and directors in Christian and Yazidi towns. In Baghdad in 2025, gunmen from Kataib Hezbollah's state brigades raided an agriculture office to keep their ally in charge, and three people were killed.

Money flows the same way: about $2.5 billion was taken from a tax account through fake refunds, with the director of the prime minister's office among those convicted.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Iraq 8.5 out of 10 for officials working for criminal or outside interests and about 3 for its courts and watchdogs. For Iraqis this means their taxes pay militias that follow a foreign cleric, those militias run ministries, a state company and local councils, and Christian and Yazidi towns can have their officials removed by an armed group's party.

Jamaica.d:
In Jamaica the documented case of an outside party reaching inside government involves money from a company that did business with the state. In 2006 the oil trader Trafigura, which lifted oil for the Jamaican government, paid $31 million into an account linked to the governing party. The party called it a donation and said it was returned. Dutch prosecutors investigated the payment as possible bribery of officials.

The concern in a case like this is that a firm paid the people in charge of the government it was earning from, so that decisions on its business could go its way.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Jamaica 7.5 out of 10 for officials working for criminal interests and just over 5 for the strength of its courts and watchdogs. For people in Jamaica this means a firm holding government oil business paid into an account tied to the party running that government, and the question of whether it was a bribe was taken up by prosecutors in the Netherlands.

Kenya.d:
In Kenya the documented reach into the state comes from drug traffickers moving heroin through the port of Mombasa, and from a smuggling trade that drew in army units sent to fight in Somalia.

The traffickers have bought protection where they needed it: police to look away, and prosecutors and judges to stall cases. The clearest proof came from the traffickers themselves: the Akasha brothers, who ran a Mombasa heroin business, admitted in a US court that they had paid Kenyan judges, prosecutors and police for two years to block their extradition, and none of those officials has been named or charged in Kenya.

A rights group has also accused army units fighting al-Shabaab in Somalia of sharing in a sugar and charcoal smuggling trade with the militants, so that the troops' trade helped fund the group they were sent to fight; the military denies it.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Kenya 8 out of 10 for officials working for criminal interests. For Kenyans this means the judges, prosecutors and police paid by traffickers have still not faced a court at home.

Kosovo.d:
In Kosovo the documented case of an outside party getting inside the state comes from a foreign government working through Kosovo's own security services. In 2018 Turkey's government had Kosovo's police and intelligence service seize six Turkish nationals it wanted and hand them over to Ankara. This was done without the knowledge of Kosovo's own prime minister.

The case shows how a foreign state can use people inside another country's police and intelligence to act for it, without going through that country's elected government.

The Global Organized Crime Index does not score Kosovo separately; North Macedonia's figures, 6.5 out of 10 for officials working for criminal interests and just over 5 for courts and watchdogs, stand in for it here. For people in Kosovo this means the police and intelligence officers meant to protect them have acted for another government, and their elected leaders were not told.

Latvia.d:
Latvia has been reached from outside in two ways: Russia's security services recruiting inside its parliament and politics, and private bank owners paying the official who supervised them. The record now shows Russia's FSB, its main security service, working through elected politicians over many years, both through the parties that speak for the country's large Russian-speaking minority and beyond them.

Leaked emails published in 2024 show Tatjana Ždanoka, who represented Latvia in the European Parliament for twenty years and co-led the Latvian Russian Union party, reporting to FSB officers from at least 2004; Latvia's security service has opened a criminal case but she has not been convicted. Jānis Ādamsons, a former interior minister who sat on parliament's defence and anti-corruption committee, was convicted in 2023 of passing material on NATO units and on Latvia's own security service to the FSB through a former KGB officer, after more than 100 meetings from at least 2015.

Bank owners have reached the top of the regulator. In 2023 a court jailed the former governor of the Bank of Latvia, who also sat on the European Central Bank's governing council, for six years for taking a bribe from a Riga bank's shareholders in return for help with the financial regulator.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Latvia 2.5 out of 10 for officials working for outside interests and above 7.5 for its courts and watchdogs. For people in Latvia, this means that MPs sitting on the committees that oversee their police and security service have been working for the neighbouring power those services guard against, and the official meant to keep banks honest with their money was for sale to a bank's owners. Courts and investigators here have caught them, but years after the fact.

Libya.d:
Libya is split between a government in Tripoli and the forces of Khalifa Haftar in the east, and on both sides armed groups have become the state bodies that are meant to police them. In Tripoli, militias formed in 2011 have been given official status as security agencies while staying loyal to their own commanders. One, Radaa, has held the capital's only commercial airport and its prisons as a state force; another, the Stability Support Apparatus, was placed under the Presidential Council in 2021 while its chief's associates controlled the internal security agency, public companies and transfers from the central bank. After his killing in May 2025 set off fighting, the prime minister calls the militias 'a state within the state'.

Smuggling networks have their own people in coast guard units, ports and fuel distribution, so the officials who should stop fuel, migrants and drugs leaving are the ones moving them. The Sentry, an investigative group, estimates that about $20 billion of subsidised fuel was diverted in 2022–24.

Religious movements and foreign backers reach in alongside the armed groups. Followers of a Saudi cleric whose Salafi teaching demands obedience to rulers, known as Madkhalis, hold strong positions in a Tripoli security force and in Haftar's army and run the eastern mosques authority.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Libya 9.5 out of 10 for officials working for criminal interests and below 2 for the strength of its courts and watchdogs. For Libyans this means the airport, the prisons and the police in their district may answer to a militia commander rather than the law, they pay for a fuel subsidy that is resold abroad, and migrants picked up at sea can find themselves held by the people trafficking them.

Madagascar.d:
Madagascar's documented outside reach comes through elections, from a foreign network that courts several candidates at once. In the 2018 presidential race, political strategists tied to Yevgeny Prigozhin, the businessman behind the Russian private military company Wagner, worked with as many as eight candidates, offering cash or promises of money, according to the Russian outlet Proekt and the BBC; the winner denied being Russia's candidate and no evidence showed he took Russian money.

This is the approach Prigozhin's network used across much of Africa: back several contenders, so that whoever wins may owe something. In Madagascar it met a state that the Global Organized Crime Index rates as highly exposed, with officials often serving criminal or outside interests and weak courts, police and watchdogs to check them.

That weakness is why no Malagasy court or official inquiry has set out who took money or what was promised in return. For Malagasy voters it means they chose a president in a race where a foreign network was paying or courting candidates, and they have no official record of which of the people they elected, if any, owe that network anything.

Mali.d:
In Mali, the outside forces that reach into the state are mostly cocaine traffickers crossing the Sahara and the Sahel, the dry belt south of it, together with the armed groups and officials who protect them. Where the routes cross desert airstrips and border posts, traffickers pay local officials and armed groups to let the cargo through, and the UN Office on Drugs and Crime has found that the traffickers include members of the political elite and armed-group leaders. The clearest single example is the 2009 'Air Cocaine' flight, a Boeing 727 from Venezuela unloaded at a northern desert strip under protection investigators traced to local officials and armed groups; no senior figure was convicted.

Since the army took power, the military government has presented foreign intelligence as the main threat from inside. Having broken with France and turned to Russia for military support from 2021, it arrested two generals and a French national in August 2025, saying he acted for French intelligence to turn officers, politicians and civil-society figures against it; more than 30 soldiers and officials were reportedly detained. France has not commented, and the charges have not been tested in an open court.

The Global Organized Crime Index rates Mali's courts, police and watchdogs among the weakest in the world and finds officials widely serving criminal interests. For people in Mali this means that traffickers and the officials who shelter them are rarely brought to court, that drug money pays armed groups fighting in the areas where they live, and that officers or critics accused of working for a foreign power are judged by the same military government that accuses them.

Mauritius.d:
Outsiders have reached into Mauritius in two ways on the record: foreign builders paying officials for public contracts, and a foreign financier getting close to the head of state while seeking a licence from the state.

The contract route runs through middlemen. The money passes through agents or consultants, so the official who decides the contract never appears on the company's books. The African Development Bank, which lends for infrastructure, found that a Danish power-plant builder had more likely than not paid members of the Mauritian administration in this way during the tenders for the state electricity company's Saint-Louis power station, and barred it from its projects for nearly two years. That is a lender's decision, not a court verdict, and it names no Mauritian official.

The second case reached the presidency. President Ameenah Gurib-Fakim was vice-chair of a charity run by an Angolan banker, Álvaro Sobrinho, and used its credit card for private spending while he was seeking a banking licence from the Mauritian financial regulator, which she asked to issue it. After a newspaper published her card statements in 2018 she repaid the money and resigned, and the government set up a commission of inquiry into her conduct.

The Global Organized Crime Index finds a moderate level of officials serving outside interests in Mauritius and rates its institutions in the middle range. For Mauritians this means part of the electricity they pay for comes from a station whose builder was found to have paid officials, and their head of state was spending a licence-seeker's money while pressing the regulator on his behalf. No official has been named in the power case, so people do not know whether those involved are still in the public service.

Monaco.d:
The cases that touch Monaco come from the international bodies and wealthy foreign residents who base themselves there. The principality hosts sports federations and some of the world's richest people, and the documented problems arise where their money meets the decisions made in Monaco.

The clearest case is World Athletics, the governing body of track and field, which has its headquarters in Monaco. Its former president, Lamine Diack, was convicted in France of taking money from Russian sports officials to delay doping cases against Russian athletes, so that suspected dopers could compete at the 2012 London Olympics. In the second case, Dmitry Rybolovlev, a Russian billionaire who owns the AS Monaco football club, was suspected of courting Monaco officials, including a former public prosecutor; the case was closed after the courts ruled that the phone messages it rested on had been obtained unlawfully, so no court has decided whether officials were influenced.

The Global Organized Crime Index finds a fairly low level of officials serving outside interests in Monaco. For people there, the athletics case shows a body run from their city selling decisions to a foreign state, at the expense of athletes everywhere who competed clean. The Rybolovlev case leaves residents with no finding either way on whether a wealthy resident could buy favour from their prosecutors.

Mozambique.d:
Mozambique has been reached from outside by foreign lenders and contractors who paid its officials, and by criminal gangs that have police and justice staff on their side.

The clearest case is the 'hidden debts'. Foreign banks, including Credit Suisse and Russia's VTB, lent about 2 billion dollars to three state companies for fishing and maritime security projects with Privinvest, an Emirati-Lebanese shipbuilder, under state guarantees kept from parliament and the International Monetary Fund. US prosecutors said hundreds of millions went in bribes and kickbacks to bankers and Mozambican officials, the former finance minister was convicted in the United States, and Mozambique's own constitutional council declared the loans void. The arrangement depended on a few officials signing guarantees in the state's name without telling the bodies meant to approve them.

Crime groups also have people inside the bodies meant to stop them. In Maputo, kidnapping gangs have had police officers and justice staff on their side, so some of the people meant to investigate abductions were themselves taking part in them.

The Global Organized Crime Index finds officials in Mozambique serving criminal interests to one of the highest degrees anywhere. For Mozambicans the hidden loans meant debt their parliament never approved. When the loans came to light in 2016, the IMF and World Bank froze support, and one study estimated that two million people were pushed into poverty. Families in Maputo whose relatives are abducted cannot be sure the police investigating are not working with the kidnappers.

Nepal.d:
The documented cases of outsiders getting inside Nepal's state come from crime networks, a foreign spy service and a foreign company, and they work through the politicians and officials who control the borders, customs and state purchases.

Crime networks reach in through the same people who make and enforce the law. In the 1990s an MP who held ministerial posts was reported to work with D-Company, Dawood Ibrahim's Indian crime syndicate, and with Pakistan's ISI spy agency, in gun-running, forgery and sheltering fugitives, a claim never tested in court. The current case is a gold-smuggling network: Nepal's anti-graft commission charged 28 people in 2026, including the chief customs administrator at Kathmandu's international airport and a former Speaker of parliament, after seized gold was swapped out of the sealed customs warehouse.

A foreign firm selling to the state has paid officials as well. A US aviation-services company admitted in 2024 that it had paid Nepali officials through intermediary companies to win the sale of two Airbus A330 jets to Nepal Airlines Corporation, the state airline, and paid more than $55 million to settle with US prosecutors over this and a South African deal.

The Global Organized Crime Index finds officials in Nepal widely serving criminal or outside interests and rates its institutions as weak. For Nepali people this means smuggled goods can pass the country's main airport because the officers checking them, and politicians above them, are alleged to work for the smugglers; a minister they elected was reported to be serving a foreign crime syndicate and spy service; and the state airline's purchase of aircraft, made with public money, was won with bribes to officials.

Niger.d: Niger lies on a Sahel route that the UN drugs office describes as a natural stopover for South American cocaine heading to Europe. Where a trafficking route crosses a thinly policed country, traffickers make use of local officials, whose vehicles and offices are less likely to be searched; the clearest example is a mayor caught in early 2022 with more than 200 kilograms of cocaine in his vehicle, with no outcome recorded since. Higher up, a researcher has reported that a cocaine-linked businessman known as 'Cherif Cocaine' funded the ruling party's campaigns and was protected by officials at the highest levels, though the claim is hard to document. The Global Organized Crime Index scores Niger high for officials working for criminal interests and low for the strength of its courts and police, so residents have little reason to expect a trial that shows who else was involved.

Oman.d:
The clearest documented reach into Oman's state came from Britain, and its effect is still felt: the sultan whom British officers helped put in power in 1970, Qaboos, ruled for half a century. At the time Oman's armed forces were under de facto British command. On 23 July 1970 the British commander briefed the Omani officers who carried out a palace coup in Salalah that removed Sultan Said bin Taimur and installed his son, who was then under house arrest and had been sent the plan on cassette tapes by British officials. Accounts based on British records say MI6, the Foreign Office and the Ministry of Defence planned it and the prime minister approved it; Britain denied involvement for forty years, saying its officers had acted on their own.

Nothing documented since then shows a foreign state, company, crime group or secret society with people or money inside Omani offices or firms. The Global Organized Crime Index places Oman in its moderate band, scoring it in the middle range both for officials working for criminal or outside interests and for the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs. Read together, those scores suggest that outside interests have some room to reach officials and that the bodies which would expose them are of middling strength.

For Omanis, this means the ruling line they have lived under for most of the past five decades began with a decision made largely in London, by officers commanding their own army. Today they cannot see whether contracts go to favoured firms or whether crimes linked to officials go unpunished; published court records, audits and lists of who owns the companies doing business with the state would be the first places such a pattern would show.

Papua New Guinea.d:
In Papua New Guinea, outsiders have reached officials through contracts paid for by Australia and through police who let drug flights land.

Australia's offshore asylum centre on Manus Island brought large contracts paid in Australian dollars into a country where officials decide on visas, land and permits, and a former contractor executive has alleged that some of that money reached a businessman close to senior officials, an allegation that is denied and untested. Drug traffickers using PNG as a route to Australia have relied on police help: after a plane carrying 548 kilograms of cocaine crashed near Port Moresby in 2020, the police commissioner said there are criminals in uniform in the constabulary, yet the officers alleged to have helped were not charged.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores PNG among the highest in the world for officials working for criminal interests and low for the strength of its courts and police, so residents have little reason to trust the force to police itself.

Poland.d:
In Poland, the documented cases of outsiders getting their people inside the state come mostly from Russia, Belarus and China and are aimed at the people who hold state secrets; one more came from private brokers selling faster visas.

Since 2022 Polish counter-intelligence has uncovered a series of Russian and Belarusian recruits inside the state, from a defence ministry employee who had worked there since the 1990s, detained in 2026, to a radio operator in the volunteer Territorial Defence Forces charged that year with seeking to spy for Russia. In 2024 a Warsaw judge who ruled on whether military and intelligence officers could see classified information fled to Belarus; officials say he worked for Russia, which has not been proven. Prosecutors say Chinese intelligence worked through a Huawei employee and a former Polish security officer to win access to government data systems; both deny it, and the trial is held behind closed doors.

The visa affair ran through the foreign ministry. Brokers selling faster Polish visas got their clients' names passed from the ministry to consulates for quick approval: the state audit office found that a deputy foreign minister forwarded lists of people 'third parties' wanted approved, and he has been charged with taking bribes, which he denies. Polish visas are valid across the EU's Schengen area, so people approved this way could travel across most of Europe.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Poland in the middle range for officials working for criminal interests. For Poles, this means people deciding who may see military secrets, or working beside them for decades, may have been reporting to Moscow or Minsk, much of the evidence stays out of public view, and a visa could depend on which broker an applicant paid rather than on the rules.

Russia.d:
In Russia the reach has run in two directions since the Soviet Union ended. In the 1990s, crime groups reached into the companies of a weak state; since then, the state's own security services have reached into business, sport and local government.

In the 1990s crime groups took over enterprises through their own people and ties with managers. The named leader of the Tambov crime group became deputy president of St Petersburg's main fuel company, one of up to 100 enterprises the gang controlled, and crime groups took control of the Lada carmaker's sales network through its managers.

Today the FSB, Russia's security service, can be used to settle business fights: an American investor says a rival used connections inside the FSB to have him arrested while the two were fighting over control of a bank. The same services reach into bodies meant to be independent: reports for the World Anti-Doping Agency found that the sports ministry and the FSB ran a state system through the Moscow testing laboratory that hid doped athletes, protecting more than 1,000 Russian competitors between 2011 and 2015. In the regions, criminal gangs have operated for years under the protection of local police and officials, in one town until its members murdered 12 people.

For Russians, a business can be lost through an arrest rather than a court case the owner could win, and in some regions the police have protected gangs rather than the people they threatened. The Global Organized Crime Index gives Russia one of the highest scores in the world for officials working for criminal interests and low marks for its courts and watchdogs.

Sao Tome and Principe.d:
São Tomé and Príncipe is a small island state in the Gulf of Guinea that shares an offshore oil zone with Nigeria, and its one recorded case of outsiders reaching in comes from the race for those oil rights. ERHC, a small Houston oil company controlled from 2001 by a Nigerian businessman who was a major donor to Nigeria's ruling party, obtained unusually favourable terms, including the right to pick the best blocks without the usual fee. In 2005 São Tomé's attorney general reported that bidding in the shared zone showed serious procedural deficiencies and political manipulation and that ERHC may have made improper payments to government officials. The FBI raided ERHC's Houston offices in 2006, the company denied wrongdoing, and no charges were reported.

The Sovereign Military Order of Malta, a Catholic order with diplomatic relations with many states, is also present; that is lawful and not evidence of wrongdoing. The Global Organized Crime Index scores the country low for officials working for criminal or outside interests, though its courts, police and watchdogs are also rated below the middle of the scale, which means fewer bodies able to find outside pressure if it were there.

For people in São Tomé and Príncipe, this means the oil under their waters, potentially the country's largest source of income, was parcelled out in a process their own attorney general found manipulated, and no court has said who was paid. They are best protected when they can see who wins resource rights and public contracts and who owns the companies that hold them.

Seychelles.d:
Little has been proven about outsiders reaching into the Seychelles state, and what has been reported centres on the heroin that moves through the islands of the western Indian Ocean. People who use drugs, prison staff and former anti-narcotics officers interviewed for research published in 2021 described police who release dealers after a payment, resell seized drugs and protect some traffickers while pursuing their rivals, and they said corruption in the anti-narcotics bureau reaches high. A parliamentary committee separately found irregular payments of about US$6 million, involving the drug-enforcement agency and the financial intelligence unit, sent to offshore companies in Mauritius.

None of this has been tested in court: as of 2021 the Anti-Corruption Commission had no active case of drug-related corruption. The Global Organized Crime Index scores state-embedded crime here at 4 out of 10 and the strength of courts, police and watchdogs at about 5.4, both near the middle of the scale.

For residents this means the agencies they are told are fighting the drug trade are described as compromised by the people who work closest to them, while no court has yet said who was paid or by whom. In a 2017 survey by the Anti-Corruption Commission, more than four in five of the roughly 15,000 people who answered said corruption was very high.

Slovenia.d:
The documented attempts from outside to get inside Slovenia's state have come through two doors: arms buying, where a single contract is large and the details are kept from the public, and the office that prosecutes organised crime. In 2006 Patria, a Finnish state-owned arms maker, won a deal worth 278 million euros to supply 135 armoured vehicles, and the Finnish broadcaster YLE later alleged that bribes were paid partly aimed at Prime Minister Janez Janša. A Slovenian conviction of Janša was annulled by the Constitutional Court and the case lapsed; defendants in Finland were acquitted and one middleman was convicted in Austria. No court has a standing finding that Janša took money, and he denies it.

Organised crime has reached the prosecutors themselves. In 2021 police said an official who had worked for about five years in the Specialised State Prosecutor's Office, which handles organised crime, had photographed files on live investigations, including orders for house searches and covert surveillance, and passed them through her partner to the Slovenian cell of the Kavač clan, a Montenegrin cocaine-trafficking syndicate. Two of the cell's key members avoided arrest, and the official had passed every background check.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores state-embedded crime here at 6.5 out of 10, higher than most of its EU neighbours, and the strength of courts, police and watchdogs at about 6.2. For Slovenians this means an organised-crime investigation can reach the gang it targets before the police knock on the door, taxpayers paid for the country's largest arms purchase while a foreign broadcaster said it had been won with bribes, and voters have judged the prime minister at several elections since without a final answer from any court.

South Sudan.d:
No documented case for South Sudan yet meets the map's test of an outside party getting its people, money or control inside a government body and having decisions there serve it.

The wider picture suggests the risk is high. Oil is the state's main income, and Glencore admitted in a UK court in 2022 to paying bribes for oil business in five African countries, South Sudan among them. The Global Organized Crime Index scores state-embedded crime here at 9 out of 10 and courts, police and watchdogs at about 2, among the worst in the world.

For South Sudanese this means that if oil revenue or state contracts are being steered by outside payments, there are few courts, police units or watchdogs able to find out or to act.

St. Lucia.d:
Nothing is documented here, so this is an estimate. No case has been found of foreign governments, companies or criminal groups paying or placing officials in St Lucia.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores state-embedded crime here at 3 out of 10, which is low, and the strength of courts, police and watchdogs at about 5.5, near the middle of the scale. The main risk in the eastern Caribbean is the cocaine route north from South America, which passes through these islands.

For residents, the absence of a documented case means there is no known instance of officials here being paid or placed from outside. It also means the estimate rests on the index's own assessment rather than on any investigation or court case in St Lucia, and it would change if a case came to light, most likely through the drug route.

Sweden.d:
In Sweden the reach into the state comes from two directions: criminal networks working through ordinary public administration, and foreign intelligence services recruiting people inside Sweden's own security agencies.

The criminal route is the larger one today. A 2023 research review for the SNS think tank found that criminal networks have people inside government agencies, run companies in the welfare sector, such as home care, schools and assistance services, and draw on social insurance; wrong welfare payments are estimated at 13 to 16 billion kronor a year. Municipalities are most exposed, because they spend much of the money with less oversight. Courts have convicted police employees of passing data from police registers to these networks, and police reporting calls insider access a systematic weakness.

Russian military intelligence, the GRU, has placed agents inside the Swedish state in two separate generations. During the Cold War an air force colonel in the defence minister's office passed it about 20,000 pages including Sweden's air defence plans, and from 2011 to 2021 a man who had worked for both the Security Service and military intelligence passed it information for money, for which he was jailed for life in 2023.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores state-embedded crime here at 2 out of 10 and courts and watchdogs at about 7.4. For Swedes this shows where the problem lies: their taxes fund welfare companies that criminal groups run, the losses fall on municipal budgets for care and schools, people who report crimes can be identified to the groups they reported from inside the police, and the agencies meant to catch foreign spies have themselves been penetrated.

Tajikistan.d:
Tajikistan's long border with Afghanistan is one of the main routes for Afghan heroin and hashish heading north to Russia and Europe, and the drug trade reaches into the officials who are meant to stop it: border guards, police, diplomats and, by some accounts, the head of the agency created to fight it. Analysts and diplomats cited by EurasiaNet in 2012 said some estimate drug money at the equivalent of 30% of the economy, and that major traffickers enjoy high-level protection.

The record shows how far up it can go. In 2000 Kazakh security officers seized about 62 kilograms of heroin near Almaty from two cars, one of them the Tajik ambassador's, and arrested him. In 2004 the head of the national Drug Control Agency, a former commander of the presidential guard, was jailed for life on charges that included drug trafficking; many saw the arrest as political, though critics who accepted that it was also said he had links to the trade. Lower down, in 2012 a military court jailed five officers of a border unit on the Afghan frontier after the checkpoint chief was caught with 20 kilograms of hashish.

Apart from that one disputed case, convictions stop at the level of local officers, and most seizures are of small dealers. The Global Organized Crime Index scores state-embedded crime here at 9 out of 10, among the highest in the world, and the strength of courts, police and watchdogs at about 2.5.

For people in Tajikistan this means the border is a route rather than a barrier, police and prison guards are reported to control street and prison sales, and if drug money makes up a large share of the economy, many families depend on it for work while officials who refuse to go along are at risk.

Togo.d:
Togo's one documented case of outsiders reaching into its government comes from a foreign conglomerate and the country's main economic asset, the deep-water port of Lomé. French investigators allege that subsidiaries of the Bolloré Group, the conglomerate of the French billionaire Vincent Bolloré, provided President Faure Gnassingbé's 2010 election campaign with communications work at below its real price through its advertising agency, and that the group then secured control of the port. Bolloré admitted the facts in 2021 under a guilty-plea procedure, but a Paris court refused the deal, and in 2026 he was ordered to stand trial in Paris. A similar arrangement is alleged in Guinea. The group sold its African ports business in 2022.

The Global Organized Crime Index puts Togo in its high band, scoring it 7.5 out of 10 for officials working for criminal or outside interests and about 4.4 out of 10 for the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs, below the middle of the range. Read together, those scores suggest outside interests have room to reach officials and the bodies that would expose them are weak.

For Togolese, this means the concession to run the port through which much of their trade passes is alleged to have been handed to a company that helped the president win re-election, a family that has held the presidency since 1967. The case is being tried in France, and no Togolese court has examined it, so residents depend on a foreign trial to learn how the deal was made.

Turkiye.d:
In Turkey, secret networks inside the army, police and courts have shaped the state for more than a century. The Gülen movement, a religious network led by the preacher Fethullah Gülen, placed its followers as judges, prosecutors, police and military officers. Courts have found that its followers obtained leaked questions for state entrance exams so that members would be hired.

The government blames those followers for the failed coup of July 2016 and dismissed about 150,000 people, including about a third of the judges in one day, without a court ruling on each. For most of those dismissed the evidence of membership was never tested, and other religious networks are reported to be filling the gaps: journalists report that the Menzil Sufi order has filled many emptied police posts, which the government denies, and leaked files suggest that a religious youth foundation close to the family of President Erdoğan listed its members as candidates for the armed forces, police and judiciary, which it calls forged.

A second pattern links police and politicians to crime groups and armed movements, among them the Grey Wolves, the ultranationalist youth wing of the MHP, now the president's partner in government. In 2023 nine senior Ankara police officers were suspended over ties to a crime boss, and in 2026 seven Istanbul police officers and a court clerk were held for warning a gang that recruits teenagers of raids.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal interests at 9 out of 10. For people in Turkey this means the state jobs and courtrooms they deal with have been staffed by whichever religious network held the hiring, a crime group can count on friends in the police and courts, and a public servant can lose a career on an accusation of hidden loyalty.

Ukraine.d:
Ukraine is fighting Russia while networks reach into its parliament, security services, state companies and border posts. The deepest reach is Russia's own, running through the security service since well before the full invasion. People charged as Russian agents inside the SBU, Ukraine's main security service, have included a major general said to have worked for the FSB since 2014, senior officers of its Kherson and Kharkiv offices accused of helping Russian troops in 2022, and the colonel who had headed the staff of its own Anti-Terrorist Center, sentenced to life in 2026. In 2024 two colonels in the State Guard, which protects the president, were detained over an FSB plan to kill him. In parliament, at least three sitting MPs, among them the leader of the main pro-Kremlin party, have been charged with treason.

The other lasting pattern is business circles reaching state firms and ministries for a cut. In 2025 the National Anti-Corruption Bureau said a group led by a businessman and friend of President Zelensky took about $100 million in kickbacks from contractors of Energoatom, the state nuclear power company, and it has charged a former deputy prime minister with seeking flats far below market price from a Kyiv developer in return for help with a land plot, which he denies. Customs and border officers in the west have been charged with running smuggling channels into the EU.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal interests at 8 out of 10. For Ukrainians, this means the officers meant to protect them and their leaders may be passing information to the army invading them, and kickbacks at the nuclear company raise the cost of keeping electricity on while Russia bombs the grid.

Uruguay.d:
Uruguay has strong courts and watchdogs by world standards, and no current case shows outside groups with people inside its government. The Global Organized Crime Index puts it in the Low band, scoring officials acting for criminal interests at 3.5 out of 10 and the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs at 7.5.

The documented case of outside reach comes from the years of military rule, when a foreign religious movement bought its way into the financial system. In 1981 the Unification Church, the Korean-founded movement of Sun Myung Moon, bought 49% of Banco de Crédito, one of the country's oldest banks, and started a daily newspaper that declared itself 'fully identified' with the military government. A later parliamentary commission found that the bank had lent about US$100 million, about a sixth of all its loans, to companies linked to Moon's movement before it closed in 2002.

The effect is still felt by Uruguayans who kept their savings in that bank or depended on its stability: a foreign group that owned almost half of it used depositors' money to fund its own companies, under a government that faced no free press or opposition able to ask questions. That case is the reason the risk is not zero, but in present-day Uruguay the courts, parliament and press are able to investigate such an arrangement if it happened again.

Venezuela.d:
In Venezuela the state has been accused of becoming a channel for drug trafficking, run by the military circle that took power with Hugo Chávez, and its security partly run by Cuban officers. Chávez built a secret movement inside the army from 1982 and, once elected, put fellow plotters in charge of intelligence. Since 2008 the United States has named officers from that circle, including intelligence chiefs, as working for the FARC, the Colombian guerrilla army funded by cocaine; US prosecutors call the network 'Cartel de los Soles', though analysts dispute that it is an organised cartel. Nicolás Maduro, seized by US forces in January 2026, has pleaded not guilty.

Cuba's reach went deepest. Under secret agreements from 2008, Cuban officers rebuilt Venezuela's military counterintelligence, which then watched Venezuela's own soldiers, and Cuban officers worked in the security around Maduro himself: Cuba says 32 of them were killed in the US raid. Criminals also held state functions: the prison ministry left the leader of the Tren de Aragua gang in charge of Tocorón prison, its headquarters until 2023. Foreign companies have bought their way into the state's money: a US asphalt trader admitted paying officials of PDVSA, the state oil company, for inside information and to steer contracts to a company it chose, and a Spanish telecoms group's Venezuelan arm paid officials for access to rationed dollars.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal interests at 9 out of 10 and courts, police and watchdogs at 1.9. For Venezuelans this has meant anti-drug agencies led by men accused of working for traffickers, soldiers watched under foreign supervision, prisons run by the gang inside them, oil contracts handed out for bribes, and no domestic court able to examine any of it.

Zimbabwe.d:
In Zimbabwe the documented reach-in runs through the gold trade, the country's main source of hard currency, where smuggling and laundering networks have had state officials on their side. In 2020 a gold smuggling case reached the state's spy agency and police, whose officers worked for a syndicate moving gold out through the main airport.

In 2023 undercover reporters recorded brokers, among them a preacher whom the president had appointed ambassador-at-large and presidential envoy, apparently offering to use their positions to bring illicit cash into the country, swap it for gold and sell the gold abroad as clean money. The government's financial intelligence unit said it found no evidence for the claims, and a commission was appointed.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal interests in Zimbabwe at 8 out of 10 and its courts, police and watchdogs at 3. For Zimbabweans this means gold dug from their land can leave the country with help from the officers meant to stop it, and can be used to clean criminal money abroad, with the president's own envoy filmed offering the service.
